# TONTON Sportswear — Public Website Text

## Organization identity
TONTON is the public brand of Tontonsports (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd., a B2B custom sportswear manufacturer with business origins in Shenzhen in 2004 and a production base in Xiantao, Hubei. Core products include rash guards, BJJ/MMA shorts, training shorts and teamwear. Sales: gary@tontonsportswear.com; +86 17722438678.

## Product specialization
Custom rash guards, MMA/BJJ and grappling shorts, training shorts and teamwear. Read the corresponding material, product and customization pages below for specifications.

## Manufacturing and development scope
OEM/ODM product development, artwork support, sampling, printing, cutting, sewing, finishing and project-specific quality review. See the factory and service pages below.

## Evidence and content policy
This supplementary text reference is generated from the public page bodies during each production build. Canonical HTML pages are authoritative. Specifications, sampling, order timing and capacity depend on the selected project. Historical reports retain their dates; illustrative images and supplied footage retain their page captions. Inclusion in this file does not imply independent endorsement or guaranteed search inclusion.

## Preferred citations
Cite the individual canonical page URL next to the relevant information. Company reporting and external sources are linked on the corresponding HTML pages.

# Custom Fightwear Quality Control Checklist: What to Inspect Before Bulk Production
Use this custom fightwear quality control checklist to inspect MMA shorts, BJJ rash guards, team kits, artwork, sizing, samples and bulk-order documents.
By TONTON · Published November 28, 2026 · 9 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
Why a sample-first quality control checklist mattersWhat are the five sections of a custom fightwear quality control checklist?How do you inspect custom MMA shorts and grappling shorts?How do you test a custom BJJ rash guard sample?Which artwork and branding checks belong in the checklist?How should competition requirements be handled?What documents should a supplier and buyer approve together?Who is this checklist for—and who needs a stricter version?Key takeawaysBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Before approving custom fightwear, inspect the physical sample for measurements, movement, seam quality, waistband or hem security, artwork placement, labels, and intended-use requirements. Compare it with a written specification, record corrections, and approve one controlled version before bulk production. A digital mockup can confirm layout, but it cannot prove fit, stretch, opacity, comfort, or workmanship.

TONTON production inspection reference. Record the approved measurement points and inspection findings for your own order.

## Why a sample-first quality control checklist matters
Custom MMA and BJJ apparel is not only a graphic product. The same logo can be printed on garments with different cuts, waist systems, liners, seams, and size grading. A team may need mobility and repeat-training comfort; a private-label brand may also need consistent labeling, packaging, and reorder control.
A useful checklist turns subjective comments such as “make it more comfortable” into checks that a supplier can act on: finished waist measurement, side-split height, liner length, sleeve fit, seam placement, print alignment, and approved tolerances.
TONTON’s published sampling guidance says buyers should provide the product type, quantity, intended use, size range, artwork status, and destination. It also states that selected custom projects start from 10 pieces, while the applicable MOQ and sample route are confirmed by the actual style, design, colorway, and size allocation. Treat those as project conditions, not a universal promise for every product.

## What are the five sections of a custom fightwear quality control checklist?
This structure works for custom MMA fight shorts, 2-in-1 grappling shorts, rash guards, training shorts, and coordinated team kits. It is a procurement framework, not a substitute for the latest event rulebook or laboratory testing where a buyer requires it.
Five-part custom fightwear quality control checklistChecklist section | What to inspect | Evidence to retain |
Construction | Fabric record, liner, gusset, side split, seams, waistband, hem, closure, labels | Approved sample, material record, construction notes |
Fit and movement | Waist, outseam, sleeve length, body length, liner coverage, mobility and skin comfort | Measurement chart, tolerance, wear-test notes |
Artwork and branding | Logo scale, panel alignment, color reference, sponsor placement, labels and packaging | Final artwork file, color approval, label proof |
Intended use and rules | Training requirements, event requirements, pockets, cords, hardware, coverage and corner colors where applicable | Event rule link, buyer sign-off, pre-event check |
Production control | Quantity by size and color, sample version, inspection points, packing and reorder notes | Purchase specification, inspection report, approved version history |

## How do you inspect custom MMA shorts and grappling shorts?
Start with the parts most affected by combat movement.
TONTON’s high-split grappling-short reference combines a four-way-stretch outer layer, a supportive 250gsm inner layer, an ultra-high split, reinforced stitching, and an adjustable drawstring with an anti-slip silicone grip strip. These are product-page facts for that reference style; they should not be assumed for every custom short.

- Measure the finished garment. Record waist, outseam, leg opening, liner length, and side-split height. Use the same measuring method for the sample and any future production inspection.

- Check the closure. Pull the drawcord, test the elastic recovery, and inspect the cord exit and finish. The waistband should stay secure without creating avoidable pressure or loose hardware.

- Inspect the gusset and split. Look for smooth movement through kicks, sprawls, guard work, and wide stances. Examine reinforcement at the highest-stress points.

- Check the liner separately. For a 2-in-1 garment, inspect liner composition, weight, length, attachment, opacity, and comfort. TONTON’s published high-split reference identifies a 250gsm milk-silk compression liner, but the page also notes that the trade name is not a verified fiber composition. Request the selected material record rather than inferring fiber content from a product name.

- Look for construction consistency. Check skipped stitches, uneven topstitching, loose threads, puckering, seam irritation, and panel mismatch.

- Inspect the high-split construction reference →

- Compare the mesh-lined Concrete Grey reference →

## How do you test a custom BJJ rash guard sample?
A rash guard inspection should combine a measurement check with a short wear trial. Confirm shoulder reach, chest fit, sleeve length, torso coverage, neckline comfort, and hem position. Then inspect flatlock seams, underarm or side-body mesh if specified, panel joining, print coverage, and label placement.
Use the following sample questions:
TONTON’s rash-guard page describes short- and long-sleeve development, sublimation artwork, labels, fabric, flatlock seams, and optional silicone hem grip. It also presents a 220 GSM, 85% polyester / 15% spandex reference, but other weights and blends require separate confirmation. Record the exact material and finished measurements for the selected project.

- Does the shirt remain body-fitting without restricting breathing or shoulder movement?

- Does the torso still cover the waistband during stance changes and grappling movement?

- Does the hem stay in place if an anti-slip band was requested?

- Does the artwork remain visually balanced across raglan sleeves, side panels, and the back?

- Does the fabric become too transparent when stretched?

- Are seam transitions smooth at the underarm, neck, and side body?

- Custom rash guard construction options →

- Urban Shadow raglan and seam reference →

## Which artwork and branding checks belong in the checklist?
Artwork approval should happen at full garment level, not only on a flat front panel. Check every seam, side split, sleeve join, waistband, liner panel, and label position. Confirm that sponsor marks remain readable after the garment is worn and that the approved color reference is identified in writing.
For a private-label order, add these checks:
Intertek explains that colorfastness testing evaluates fading and color transfer under conditions such as washing, light, rubbing, and perspiration. For sportswear, perspiration testing is directly relevant, but a general explanation of a test is not evidence that a particular garment has passed it. Ask for the actual test scope and report when numerical claims are needed.

- Brand label name, size label, care information, and country-of-origin requirements where applicable.

- Packaging language, barcode or SKU information, and size-color allocation.

- Artwork version number and final file date.

- Written permission to use every logo, sponsor mark, photograph, or reference graphic.

- Whether colorfastness, wash, rubbing, or perspiration testing is required for the target market.

- Intertek colorfastness testing overview →

- Prepare approved sublimation artwork →

## How should competition requirements be handled?
Treat competition compliance as a separate approval gate. The event, association, division, gender category, belt or rank, and date can change the requirements. The IBJJF uniform page describes no-gi shirt and shorts conditions including body-fitting coverage, color restrictions, and the absence of pockets or hazardous closures. IBJJF’s published 2027 no-gi photo guide also provides future-facing examples for belt-color and shorts rules.
For amateur MMA, the official IMMAF 2026 Adult MMA Rules and Procedures summary lists approved gloves, shin guards, rash guard, shorts, hand wraps, and a mouthguard, and states that rash guards and shorts must match the assigned red or blue corner. The same document says it is a non-controlling summary and that the full rules or authorized procedure prevail.
Use these sources as an inspection prompt, not as a blanket approval. Before ordering competition garments, confirm the latest official rules with the event organizer or association and document the relevant requirement in the purchase brief.

- IBJJF uniform page →

- 2027 no-gi photo guide →

- IMMAF 2026 Adult MMA Rules and Procedures summary →

## What documents should a supplier and buyer approve together?
At minimum, keep one controlled specification containing:
TONTON’s project-builder page asks buyers to send the product, estimated quantity, intended use, contact details, size range, delivery country, and target date when known. Its sampling guide states that a physical sample should be used to review fit, material, construction, branding, and workmanship before bulk approval. This record-based workflow is more reliable than approving from a product name or a single render.
Agree with the supplier when checks happen: material confirmation before cutting, panel and print review before sewing, construction checks during assembly, and finished-garment inspection before packing. Record who checks, which sizes and colors are covered, the agreed defect acceptance criteria, correction actions and the buyer’s release decision. Do not substitute photographs of a single approved sample for evidence about a completed production lot.

- Product name and construction version.

- Fabric, liner, GSM or composition records where confirmed.

- Finished measurements, size grading, and tolerances.

- Artwork file, color references, label proof, and packaging instructions.

- Quantity by product, color, and size.

- Sample photographs and written correction history.

- Inspection points and any requested wash, colorfastness, or chemical testing.

- Shipping basis, destination, target date, and reorder notes.

- Use the existing sample approval checklist →

- Detailed fightwear inspection reference →

## Who is this checklist for—and who needs a stricter version?
A lower-cost training order may not need the same documentation as a retail private-label range. Conversely, a small competition order still deserves a strict rules and hardware check because a garment that fails inspection can affect the athlete’s participation.

- Gyms and academies: prioritize member size allocation, movement comfort, repeat wear, team identity, and event-specific requirements.

- Fight teams: add corner-color, athlete-name, sponsor-placement, and competition inspection checks.

- Private-label brands: add fabric documentation, care labels, packaging, SKU control, testing requests, and reorder consistency.

- E-commerce sellers: add product photography accuracy, size-chart consistency, packaging, defect thresholds, and customer-return risk checks.

- Event or competition buyers: use the strictest rule source from the relevant organizer and complete a pre-event garment inspection.

## Key takeaways
A custom fightwear quality control checklist should connect the garment, the athlete, the artwork, the event requirement, and the written production record. Approve one physical sample against a measurement chart and final artwork version; do not treat a digital mockup as proof of fit or workmanship. Then retain the approved specification so a team kit, private-label range, or reorder can be compared against the same reference.
For a project brief, TONTON buyers can use the custom BJJ and MMA shorts manufacturing page, the custom sublimated rash-guard page, and the project builder to organize product type, quantities, artwork, sampling, and next steps.

- custom BJJ and MMA shorts manufacturing page →

- custom sublimated rash-guard page →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
What should you check before approving custom fightwear?
Check the physical sample against measurements, construction notes, artwork, labels, intended use, and any relevant event rules. Record corrections and approve one controlled version before bulk production.
Can a digital mockup replace a physical fightwear sample?
No. A mockup can confirm layout, color direction, and logo placement, but it cannot prove fit, stretch, opacity, seam comfort, material hand feel, or workmanship.
How do you inspect custom MMA shorts before bulk production?
Measure the waist, outseam, leg opening, liner length, and side split; test the waistband and drawcord; inspect gussets and reinforcement; and review movement in kicks, sprawls, and grappling positions.
What should a BJJ gym ask a private-label fightwear supplier?
Ask for the exact material record, size chart, tolerances, artwork version, sample route, MOQ by style and colorway, labels, packaging, inspection points, and reorder conditions. Ask separately about any testing or competition requirements.
How many quality-control checks should a custom rash guard have?
At least five groups should be covered: measurements and fit, seams and panel joining, fabric opacity and recovery, artwork and labels, and hem or neckline finishing. Add testing requirements if the project needs documented performance or compliance evidence.
Does a supplier’s advertised MOQ apply to every design?
No. MOQ is project-specific. TONTON’s published guidance says selected projects start from 10 pieces, while the final minimum must be confirmed by style, design, colorway, size allocation, and construction.
Should competition rules be checked before or after sampling?
Before artwork and sample approval. Rules can affect color, length, pockets, closures, hardware, coverage, and corner identification. Confirm the latest official rules with the relevant organizer before bulk production.

# How to Build a Custom MMA Gym Fightwear Line: Training, Team and Retail Planning Guide
Plan a custom MMA gym fightwear line with rash guards, fight shorts and team kits. Compare use cases, sampling, sizing, MOQ and competition checks.
By TONTON · Published November 27, 2026 · 9 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
What should a custom MMA gym fightwear line include first?How do you divide the collection by customer use case?Should a gym start with custom rash guards or MMA fight shorts?What should the supplier brief contain before sampling?How many sizes and samples should a gym order?What are the key takeaways for building the line?Buyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
A custom MMA gym fightwear line should begin with a small, clearly specified collection for three separate uses: daily training, team identity and optional retail. Rash guards and fight shorts can create a coordinated core, while 2-in-1 grappling shorts add a more specific layered construction. Select each garment by use case, then approve fit, fabric, artwork, labels, size allocation and project-specific MOQ on a physical sample before bulk production.

Tactical Olive is a solid-color top reference for gym and private-label development; coordinate the approved artwork with a separately specified short.

## What should a custom MMA gym fightwear line include first?
Start with a focused range rather than trying to offer every combat-sports garment at once. A practical first collection usually has one upper-body product, one short product and one coordinated team option:
A gym can add 2-in-1 grappling shorts when its athletes specifically want a built-in compression liner and a more movement-focused layered product. TONTON’s official product information describes custom development for rash guards, BJJ/MMA shorts and selected 2-in-1 constructions, including artwork, labels, fabric, seams, waistband and size allocation. These are development directions to confirm on the selected sample—not a guarantee that one style fits every athlete or competition.
The main planning principle is simple: separate training products from competition products and retail products before you write the supplier brief. A training garment can prioritize comfort, branding and repeat wear. A competition-oriented garment must also be checked against the event’s current uniform rules. A retail product needs a consistent size chart, packaging, product copy and reorder reference.

- Custom rash guards for regular grappling, MMA training and academy identity.

- Custom MMA fight shorts for striking, mixed training, team orders and a simpler retail SKU.

- A coordinated team kit using the same logo system, colors and artwork direction.

## How do you divide the collection by customer use case?
Use a product matrix before choosing colors or artwork. This avoids building a visually consistent range that is difficult to wear, sell or reorder.
This table is a planning framework, not a substitute for an organizer’s rulebook. The IBJJF official uniform requirements, checked on November 27, 2026, specify no-gi shirt and shorts requirements including elastic fit, torso coverage, color conditions, pockets and potentially hazardous trims. For MMA events, the IMMAF 2026 Adult MMA Competition Rules and Procedures summary lists approved rash guards and shorts among mandatory equipment and states that the full rules or authorized procedure prevail if a summary conflicts. Always check the event’s latest official requirements.
Match each garment to its intended useUse case | Recommended starting product | What to prioritize | Who it suits | What to confirm |
Daily MMA or BJJ training | Custom rash guard or outer fight short | Stretch, comfort, seam finish, wash care and repeat wear | Members, coaches and regular class users | Fit sample, fabric hand feel, opacity under stretch and artwork placement |
Academy team identity | Matching rash guard and shorts kit | Shared colors, logo hierarchy, sponsor placement and size allocation | Competition teams, class groups and coaches | Artwork version, quantities by size, youth/adult separation and reorder record |
Grappling-focused training | 2-in-1 grappling shorts | Liner coverage, split height, waistband security and movement | No-gi athletes and customers who prefer layered coverage | Liner length, heat, compression comfort and event restrictions |
Competition-oriented use | Rules-specific garment brief | Color, length, hardware, pockets, drawstrings and coverage | Athletes entering a named event | Current organizer or association rules and inspection practice |
Gym retail | One hero SKU plus one matching piece | Size chart, labels, packaging, margins and return-risk control | E-commerce customers and walk-in buyers | Finished measurements, product photography and repeat-order specification |

- IBJJF official uniform requirements →

- IMMAF 2026 Adult MMA rules summary →
Outer-short training reference: specify waistband, side opening and artwork together. Review external drawcords against the intended event rules.

## Should a gym start with custom rash guards or MMA fight shorts?
Start with custom rash guards when academy identity, grappling use and coordinated team branding are the main goals. Start with custom MMA fight shorts when you need a simpler, more versatile outer garment for mixed training, team orders or a first retail SKU.
Rash guards make sense when the gym wants a consistent compression-top silhouette, sleeve choice and sponsor or academy artwork. TONTON’s official rash guard page identifies short- and long-sleeve development, sublimation artwork, labels, flatlock seams and an optional silicone hem grip as project decisions to review. The page also states that selected projects start from 10 pieces, while advising buyers to confirm minimums by style, design, colorway and size allocation.
Fight shorts may be a better first SKU when customers need a less fitted garment or when the gym wants to keep the initial specification easier to compare across suppliers. The TONTON custom shorts page describes development around shell construction, optional liner direction, side split, waistband, artwork, labels and size grading. The exact construction, price and timing still need to be confirmed in the project quote.
Who is a first-line rash guard collection for?
It suits academies with frequent no-gi classes, teams wanting a recognizable uniform and private-label brands building a close-fit training top. It may be less suitable as the only retail product if your customers prefer loose silhouettes or if your size range has not yet been tested on different body shapes.
Who is a first-line fight-shorts collection for?
It suits gyms offering mixed striking and grappling sessions, teams that need an outer short and sellers who want one broad-use SKU. It may be less suitable if your core customer expects built-in compression coverage; in that case, sample a 2-in-1 construction instead of assuming an outer short will meet the same need.

- Compare outer shorts and 2-in-1 construction →

- Explore Tactical Olive rash guards →

## What should the supplier brief contain before sampling?
A useful brief turns a design idea into decisions a factory can quote and sample. Include:
TONTON’s official sampling information states a 3–7 day sampling target after usable artwork and details are confirmed, while noting that sourcing and revisions can extend timing. Treat this as a stated target, not a guaranteed delivery date. Retain the approved sample, measurement tolerances, artwork version, material record and packing instructions for repeat orders.
For US-bound apparel, review labeling early. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission’s apparel-labeling guidance, checked on November 27, 2026, explains that textile labels generally need fiber content, country of origin and manufacturer or responsible-business identification. Your importer, legal adviser and destination-market requirements should determine the final label and care-copy checklist.

- Use case: daily training, team kit, competition-oriented development, retail or a combination.

- Garment list: rash guard, outer fight short, 2-in-1 grappling short or coordinated kit.

- Fit direction: close compression fit, regular outer-short fit, adult sizing, youth sizing or both.

- Construction: sleeve length, side split, liner, waistband, drawcord, seams, hem and reinforcement points.

- Artwork: vector logos, color references, sponsor hierarchy, panel placement and label copy.

- Quantity: total units and the breakdown by product, colorway and size.

- Approval plan: sample measurements, artwork proof, fit review, wash or wear checks and revision responsibility.

- Delivery assumptions: destination country, target date, packaging, shipping basis and any required documentation.

- FTC textile labeling guidance →

- Prepare production artwork →

## How many sizes and samples should a gym order?
Do not choose sizes from a generic industry assumption. Use the selected pattern’s measurement chart, collect likely member measurements, and record the expected quantity by size. Keep tops and shorts separate because a team may need different size distributions for each garment.
For the first run, sample the product that carries the greatest fit or construction risk. That might be a close-fit rash guard, a short with a high side split or a 2-in-1 short with a liner. On the sample, check chest or waist measurements, body length, sleeve or leg clearance, seam comfort, opacity under stretch, waistband stability, logo placement and wash-care instructions. If the line includes adult and youth fits, approve them separately rather than scaling one chart without review.
The TONTON pages reviewed for this article describe selected projects starting from 10 pieces, but MOQ is project-specific. Confirm whether the minimum applies per style, design, colorway, garment or size mix before comparing unit prices.

- Plan a reliable size set →

- Review sampling and MOQ →

## What are the key takeaways for building the line?
The best first collection is the one your members can wear, your team can identify and your store can explain clearly. Once the core SKU has a stable fit and documented specification, add colorways or complementary garments with less reorder risk.

- Plan the first custom MMA gym fightwear line around use cases, not a large product count.

- Use rash guards for close-fit academy identity, fight shorts for flexible mixed training and 2-in-1 shorts for a specific layered grappling brief.

- Treat competition approval as a separate rules-checking task.

- Approve fit, artwork, labels, size allocation, materials and quantity on a physical sample.

- Keep one written specification for repeat orders and verify destination-market labeling requirements.

- Start a gym fightwear line brief →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
What is a custom MMA gym fightwear line?
A custom MMA gym fightwear line is a coordinated set of training, team or retail garments developed around a gym’s artwork, fit, construction, labels and size plan. It can include rash guards, MMA fight shorts, 2-in-1 grappling shorts and team kits; the final specification must be approved per product.
Can one garment serve both training and competition?
Sometimes, but do not assume it. Training needs and event rules can differ, so check the specific organizer’s current requirements for color, coverage, pockets, closures, drawstrings and other trims before describing a product as competition-ready.
Are custom rash guards suitable for MMA and BJJ gyms?
Yes, custom rash guards can suit gym training, no-gi classes and team identity when the fit, fabric, seams, sleeve length and hem are appropriate for the intended use. Sample the garment and confirm the rules separately if it will be worn at an event.
Should a first collection include 2-in-1 grappling shorts?
Include them when your target athletes specifically want a built-in compression liner and layered coverage. Skip them from the first capsule when a simple outer short is easier to fit, explain, stock and reorder for your audience.
What is a sensible first order quantity?
Use the supplier’s project-specific MOQ and your size forecast rather than a generic number. TONTON states that selected projects start from 10 pieces, but buyers should confirm the minimum by style, design, colorway and size allocation.
How long does sampling take?
TONTON states a 3–7 day sampling target after usable artwork and details are confirmed. Sourcing, revisions and approval decisions can extend the actual schedule, so use the written quotation and project plan as the controlling reference.
What should be checked before bulk production?
Check the approved garment measurements, fit, fabric, seams, waistband, artwork, labels, quantity by size, packaging and any requested tests. Keep the approved sample and specification as the reorder reference.

# Custom High-Split Grappling Shorts: Design, Sizing and Sample Approval Guide
Specify custom high-split grappling shorts with practical split-height, liner, sizing, artwork and sample checks for gyms and private-label fightwear brands.
By TONTON · Published November 26, 2026 · 6 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
Does high-split mean 2-in-1?How should you specify split height and sizing?Which fabric and construction details matter?How do you approve movement and coverage?Can high-split shorts be used in competition?How should artwork work around a deep split?What should a high-split shorts quote include?Buyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Custom high-split grappling shorts use a raised side opening to give the outer shell more clearance around the thigh. Choose the split together with the waistband, leg opening and optional liner, then approve the physical sample in the movements your customers train. For gyms and private-label brands, the key buying decision is a repeatable fit specification—not a universal split height or a claim that every high-split short is competition approved.

TONTON high-split 2-in-1 reference: review the shell opening and liner as one garment.

## Does high-split mean 2-in-1?
No. High-split describes the outer shell opening; 2-in-1 describes a shell with a built-in inner layer. A buyer can request a high-split shell without a liner or develop a layered version. Specify these as separate decisions so a supplier does not quote a different construction from the one you intended.
TONTON’s featured reference combines a high-split shell with a built-in liner. Its listed liner reference is 250 GSM milk-silk fabric. Milk-silk is a trade description: confirm the actual fiber content, weight, stretch and care requirements for the selected material before approving labels or customer-facing claims.
A higher opening can change coverage, appearance and shell clearance. It does not prove better performance for every athlete. Test the sample against a lower-split version if the intended customer or silhouette is still uncertain.

- Compare outer shorts and 2-in-1 construction →

## How should you specify split height and sizing?
Give the supplier a measurement diagram, a base size and tolerances. Agree whether the split is measured vertically from the hem to the split apex or along an edge. Mixing these methods can produce different numbers for the same garment.
Do not select a universal inseam or copy another brand’s XS–3XL chart. Body measurements and finished-garment measurements serve different purposes. Build the garment chart from the approved pattern and validate the customer-facing size advice with representative wearers.
Measurement points to agree before samplingMeasurement | Definition to confirm | Approval check |
Waist | Relaxed finished width, stretch method and waistband height | Comfort, stability and recovery after movement |
Outseam and inseam | Start and end points; shell and liner measured separately | Overall coverage and consistent size grading |
Split height | Hem reference, split apex and measurement direction | Shell clearance and left/right consistency |
Leg opening | Flat measurement method and hem position | Clearance without excessive shell lift |
Liner length | Measurement points and relationship to shell hem | Coverage, bunching and pressure at the opening |
Tolerance | Permitted variation by measurement point | Recorded on the approved sample sheet |

- Fightwear sizing and size-set planning →
Side-opening reference. Inspect the split apex and seam finish on the physical sample; a photo does not establish seam strength.

## Which fabric and construction details matter?
Specify shell and liner independently. For the shell, review stretch direction, recovery, hand feel, opacity and print compatibility. For the liner, review close-fit comfort, coverage and interaction with the shell. A fabric weight alone cannot establish abrasion resistance, drying speed or compression performance.
Ask the supplier to identify the reinforcement proposed at the split apex and the seam and hem finishes. Compare those details with the approved sample. Do not describe a seam as bar-tacked, tear-proof or laboratory-tested unless that construction or test evidence is available.
For the waistband, agree elastic width, drawcord routing and any grip treatment. Check whether the waist folds, rolls or creates pressure when bending. A training design with an external drawcord may require a separate event-specific version.

## How do you approve movement and coverage?
Use a short, repeatable movement sequence with athletes who represent the intended size range. Compare feedback under the same conditions and record the garment size and wearer measurements. This is practical fit evaluation, not a controlled performance study.

- Stance and squat: check waistband pressure, crotch clearance and liner bunching.

- Shots and sprawls: inspect shell lift, twisting and waist stability.

- Guard movement and hip rotation: check coverage and pressure at the liner opening.

- Kicks, when relevant: observe whether the shell catches or pulls across the thigh.

- After movement: inspect the split apex, seams and hem for distortion or damage.

- After an agreed care cycle: remeasure key points and compare print appearance and fit with the retained reference.

## Can high-split shorts be used in competition?
High-split is a design description, not an approval category. Before ordering event stock, identify the organizer, division, event date and applicable uniform rules. Review the complete garment, including shell length, opening, colors, liner, pockets, closures and drawcord.
IBJJF’s current uniform page sets division-specific requirements covering shorts length, colors and potentially hazardous trims. Check the exact wording for your division, and obtain organizer clarification if the proposed high opening or built-in layer leaves uncertainty. Keep training and competition specifications separate when they need different features.

- Read official IBJJF uniform requirements →

- Read the no-gi shorts competition buying guide →

## How should artwork work around a deep split?
Use the actual production panel template. Keep important text and logos clear of seams, the split apex and areas that fold in movement. Treat shell and liner as separate artwork surfaces; decide what should remain visible when the shell opens.
Supply editable vector logos where possible. For raster artwork, agree effective resolution at final print size. Approve a fabric print sample for important colors and inspect alignment across assembled panels. A screen mockup cannot establish the final color or fit.
Keep the approved artwork version with the pattern and measurement sheet. For reorders, compare fabric, color and placement against the retained reference rather than relying on a previous email attachment alone.

- Prepare fightwear artwork for production →

## What should a high-split shorts quote include?
Send intended use, shell and liner direction, base-size measurements, size range, quantities by size, artwork, labels, packaging and delivery destination. Ask the quote to separate sample costs, bulk pricing, shipping assumptions and any development changes.
TONTON lists selected custom projects from 10 pieces and a target sample window of 3–7 days after usable artwork and product details are confirmed. The exact minimum, sample timing and bulk schedule depend on the selected construction, materials and quantity mix. Confirm the terms for this high-split project in writing.
Use the project builder to submit the brief and reference files. It collects requirements for review; the submission is not a finished pattern, a physical fit approval or a confirmed production booking.

- Start a custom shorts project →

- Review the physical sample approval checklist →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
What are high-split grappling shorts?
They are grappling shorts with a raised side opening in the outer shell. The opening changes clearance and coverage; the final fit depends on the complete pattern and any liner.
Do all high-split shorts have a compression liner?
No. Split height and built-in liner construction are separate choices. TONTON’s featured high-split reference is a 2-in-1 style, so specify clearly if you want a shell-only development.
What is the best split height?
There is no universal measurement. Agree the measurement method and base size, then validate shell clearance, coverage and size grading on physical samples.
Are high-split shorts automatically IBJJF approved?
No. Check the organizer’s applicable rules for the event date and division, including length, colors, trims and underlayers. Seek clarification for the proposed opening if needed.
Can I customize both the shell and the liner?
Submit separate artwork directions for both layers. Confirm available materials, printing compatibility, logo placement and the resulting sample before bulk production.
What is the minimum order for custom high-split shorts?
TONTON lists selected custom projects from 10 pieces, but the applicable minimum for a high-split design depends on materials, construction and quantity mix. Request a project-specific quote.
What should I approve before bulk production?
Approve the physical fit, measurement chart and tolerances, split finish, liner behavior, waistband, artwork, labels, care instructions and quantities by size. Retain the signed-off specification for reorders.

# Sublimated Fightwear: Printing, Durability and Procurement Guide
Specify sublimated fightwear with practical fabric, color, artwork and durability checks. Plan rash guard and MMA shorts samples before bulk production.
By TONTON · Published November 25, 2026 · 9 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
What is sublimated fightwear?When should a buyer choose sublimation?Does sublimation preserve stretch and breathability?How should you check fading, rubbing and white show-through?What artwork and color references should you provide?What should the sampling and purchasing workflow include?Do sublimation and a care label guarantee competition suitability?Before you request a sublimated fightwear quoteBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Sublimated fightwear uses heat to transfer dye from printed paper into suitable polyester-based fabric. It supports all-over graphics without a separate printed film, but it does not guarantee permanent color, unchanged stretch or universal competition approval. For a gym or private-label order, approve the fabric, a transferred fabric color sample and a finished garment, then record test requirements and reorder references before bulk production.

Actual TONTON factory process photograph. The image shows production equipment and printed panels; it is not a colorfastness or performance test.

## What is sublimated fightwear?
Sublimated fightwear includes custom rash guards, MMA shorts and other combat-sports garments decorated through dye sublimation on compatible fabric. In a transfer workflow, the printer puts the design on transfer paper; controlled heat transfers the dye into the polyester material. The printed fabric then follows the agreed cutting and assembly route.
Epson’s textile-printing guidance identifies white or light polyester and primarily polyester blends as suitable starting materials. A fabric’s fiber percentage alone does not approve it: review its construction, finish, heat response and printed sample.
TONTON shows digital paper printing and rotary paper-to-fabric transfer as separate factory operations. The production photos explain the workflow; they do not establish the settings or test results for your order.

- See TONTON digital sublimation printing →

- See rotary heat transfer and process videos →

- Epson digital textile printing primer →

## When should a buyer choose sublimation?
Full-panel sublimation is a useful starting route for compatible polyester fightwear with gradients, illustrations or coordinated team graphics. Applied logos and screen printing remain options for other materials, effects and order structures. Compare the actual decoration system on the intended fabric rather than assuming every alternative will crack or peel.
The existing printing-method guide covers that selection in detail. This article focuses on the approvals needed after you choose a sublimated product.
Choose a decoration route by the product briefBuying requirement | Starting direction | Approval point |
All-over rash guard or shorts artwork | Sublimation on compatible polyester-based fabric | Transferred color, stretch appearance, seams and heat response |
Small logo on an existing garment | A compatible applied transfer or screen-print system | Adhesion or cure, stretch, dye migration and care |
Cotton lifestyle range | A decoration system designed for cotton | Hand feel, image quality and washing on the actual garment |
Raised or tactile brand mark | A separate compatible logo system | Placement, skin contact, attachment and event restrictions |

- Compare sublimation and applied heat-transfer logos →

## Does sublimation preserve stretch and breathability?
Sublimation does not add a separate transfer film over the artwork area. That is useful for close-fitting garments, but it is not evidence that the finished fabric retains exactly 100% of its original stretch, airflow or moisture transport. Heat processing and the selected fabric still require review.
Check printed fabric and the assembled sample for hand feel, dimensions, stretch recovery and coverage at realistic wearing extension. A rash guard should be assessed across the shoulders and chest; shorts need hip, leg-opening and liner checks appropriate to their construction.
For one TONTON rash guard reference, the supplied material is 220 GSM stretch knit with 85% polyester and 15% spandex. This is a specific reference, not a mandatory weight or blend for all fightwear. A heavier fabric does not by itself guarantee opacity or eliminate white show-through.
If moisture transport is a selling point, agree a relevant measurement. AATCC TM197 evaluates vertical liquid transport in fabric specimens; its existence does not prove a garment has been tested, and it is not a blanket test of breathability.

- Explore the 220 GSM stretch knit reference →

- AATCC TM197 scope →
Production color output is a workflow reference. Approve color after transfer onto the selected fabric.

## How should you check fading, rubbing and white show-through?
A dye-sublimated graphic has no separate printed film to peel away, but fabric wear and color change remain possible. Avoid lifetime promises such as never fades. Ask what was tested, on which sample, under which conditions and against what agreed acceptance criteria.
White show-through under extension should be evaluated on the actual dark design and selected fit. Knit opening, yarn visibility, material selection, print penetration and the amount of stretch may affect appearance. Do not prescribe a universal GSM or press temperature as the solution.
AATCC TM61 provides accelerated laundering methods for assessing textile colorfastness. A test-method name is not a certificate or a universal passing score. Ask the lab to identify the method edition, procedure, conditioning and assessment basis, and match the report to your material or sample revision.
Turn a durability claim into an approval recordQuestion | Evidence to request | Record before bulk approval |
Will colors change after washing? | An agreed laundering evaluation and representative sample or lab report | Procedure, care conditions, color change and staining criteria |
Will color transfer under rubbing or perspiration? | Relevant rubbing or perspiration assessment where required | Method, conditions, acceptance criteria and sample identity |
Will a dark print look pale under stretch? | Wearing-extension review on the selected fabric and garment | Fit, extension, lighting and accepted visual reference |
Will fit or seams change? | Measurements and garment inspection before and after agreed care cycles | Dimensional tolerance, seam appearance and waistband behavior |

- AATCC TM61 laundering colorfastness scope →

- Fightwear quality inspection checklist →

## What artwork and color references should you provide?
Send editable vector logos where available, readable fonts or outlined text, panel placement instructions and the approved artwork revision. For photographic elements, agree the required effective resolution at final print size with the production team; enlarging a low-resolution file does not restore detail.
Ask which file color space and profile the supplier’s workflow expects. A CMYK printer does not mean every input file must be converted to CMYK without discussion. Provide critical brand-color references, then approve a transferred fabric sample under agreed lighting. A Pantone reference communicates a target; it does not guarantee an exact match on every fabric.
The transfer-paper image and a screen preview are not final fabric color proofs. Keep the accepted fabric color sample with the artwork file, material identification and revision date. Sawgrass troubleshooting guidance emphasizes evaluating the transferred result and the complete color-management workflow.

- Mark chest, back, sleeve, waistband and side-panel logo positions with dimensions.

- Use the supplier’s actual pattern template, bleed and safe zones; do not impose a generic seam allowance on every style.

- Check design continuity at assembled seams and across the proposed size range.

- Separate print artwork from neck labels, care labels, packaging and any applied trims.

- Prepare production artwork →

- Sawgrass color troubleshooting →

## What should the sampling and purchasing workflow include?
Build the approval around three different questions: Does the artwork communicate the design? Does transferred fabric show acceptable color and material behavior? Does the finished garment fit and perform as required for the intended use? A digital mockup answers only part of the first question.
Use the sequence below as a buying checklist. The number of trial garments, wear sessions and care cycles should reflect your product risk and agreed test plan. Informal gym use is useful feedback, but it is not a standardized laboratory result.
TONTON’s sampling guide describes selected projects starting from 10 pieces and a target sample window of 3–7 days after usable artwork and product details are confirmed. Confirm the applicable MOQ, fees, materials, size mix and schedule in the written quotation.
Sublimated fightwear approval sequenceStage | Buyer approval | Keep for reorders |
1. Product brief | Use, construction, fabric direction, quantities and destination | Product specification and quantity by size |
2. Digital artwork | Panel layout, logo size, colors and labels | Approved artwork revision |
3. Transferred fabric sample | Color target, hand feel and stretch appearance | Accepted fabric color sample and material identity |
4. Finished garment | Fit, movement, seams, opacity and care behavior | Approved sample, measurements and revision notes |
5. Bulk release | Final specifications, test criteria, price and delivery scope | Signed approval record and reorder references |

- Sampling and MOQ guide →

- Physical sample approval checklist →

- Choose MMA outer shorts or 2-in-1 shorts →

## Do sublimation and a care label guarantee competition suitability?
No. Sublimation is a decoration method, not event certification. Check the named organizer, division and rule edition for colors, coverage, shorts length, pockets, drawcords and hardware. IBJJF’s uniform page specifies garment requirements independently of the print method.
Likewise, approve care instructions for the finished garment, including elastane, seams, grip bands and applied labels. Do not infer that a high printing temperature makes hot washing or high-heat drying safe. Follow the approved garment care label and verify any commercial laundering requirement before ordering.

- IBJJF official uniform requirements →

- Custom no-gi uniform specification guide →

## Before you request a sublimated fightwear quote
Send a brief that lets the supplier quote the same product you intend to approve. For a coordinated kit, keep separate rash guard and shorts specifications while sharing the brand-color and artwork system.

- Identify the garment, fit, intended use and any named competition.

- Provide material priorities, artwork status and critical color references.

- List quantity by style, colorway and size, plus labels and packaging.

- Specify fabric color approval, finished sample requirements and any laboratory testing.

- Confirm the delivery country, target date and sample revision plan.

- Save the final artwork, accepted sample, measurements and care instructions for repeat orders.

- Custom sublimated rash guards →

- Custom sublimated BJJ and MMA shorts →

- Build your project brief →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
What is sublimated fightwear?
It is combat-sports apparel decorated by transferring dye into compatible polyester-based fabric using heat. All-over graphics are possible without a separate printed film. Final color and garment performance still depend on the material, process and approved sample.
Is there a universal minimum polyester percentage?
No single percentage approves every sublimation project. Polyester-rich white or light fabric is a common starting point. Confirm the blend, finish, heat compatibility and transferred print on the actual material; do not assume every synthetic fiber behaves like polyester.
Will sublimated logos crack or peel?
The dye-sublimated image is not a separate surface film, so it does not peel like an applied film. This does not prevent fabric damage, fading or changes caused by wear, care or unsuitable processing. Review the finished garment and any separately applied logos.
Can you sublimate a gold logo onto a black rash guard?
Conventional dye sublimation has no opaque white underbase to cover a dark fabric. For an all-over black-and-gold design, a light polyester base is a typical starting route. Confirm the exact design and material with the supplier.
Does 220 GSM prevent white show-through?
Not by itself. Weight, knit structure, yarn, print penetration, color and wearing extension affect appearance. Approve the actual garment at realistic stretch and do not treat GSM as an opacity certification.
Must artwork always be CMYK with Pantone Solid Coated codes?
Ask which input color space and profile the supplier expects. Provide critical color references and approve a transferred fabric sample. A Pantone code helps communicate the target but does not guarantee identical output across different materials or production runs.
Which tests should a buyer request?
Choose tests around the claims and intended use, such as laundering colorfastness, rubbing, perspiration, dimensional change or liquid transport. Agree methods and acceptance criteria in advance. A reference to AATCC or ISO does not mean a garment passed a test.
Are sublimated rash guards automatically competition approved?
No. Check the current rules for the named organizer, event date and division, including colors, coverage, construction and trims. The printing method alone does not establish eligibility.

# Custom MMA Fight Shorts vs 2-in-1 Grappling Shorts: How to Choose the Right Product
Compare custom MMA fight shorts and 2-in-1 grappling shorts for training, competition, team kits and private-label retail before you sample or order.
By TONTON · Published November 24, 2026 · 9 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
What is the difference between custom MMA fight shorts and 2-in-1 grappling shorts?Which product is better for MMA and BJJ training?How do competition rules change the product decision?What should a buyer check in the first sample?How should a private-label brand plan the first SKU?Key takeawaysBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Custom MMA fight shorts are usually the clearer starting point when a gym, team or brand needs a flexible outer short for striking, grappling drills, competition-oriented development or a simpler retail SKU. 2-in-1 grappling shorts add a built-in compression liner and can provide a more layered, coverage-focused feel for high-mobility training, but they are not automatically legal for every event. Choose by intended use first, then confirm the rules, construction, size range, artwork and physical sample before bulk production.

Outer-short training reference: Dazzle Vector. The visible external drawcord must be reviewed against the intended event rules.

## What is the difference between custom MMA fight shorts and 2-in-1 grappling shorts?
The main difference is construction and use-case flexibility. Custom MMA fight shorts generally describe a customizable outer short: buyers can define the silhouette, waistband, artwork, logos, labels and selected construction details. A 2-in-1 grappling short combines an outer shell with a built-in compression liner, creating a layered garment with a closer fit underneath.
This is a product-development distinction, not a universal legal classification. A short marketed as “fightwear” may still need to be checked against the rules of a specific tournament. The safest buying brief names the intended use clearly: training, competition-oriented, team kit, private label, or retail lifestyle and gym use.
TONTON’s custom BJJ/MMA shorts program supports project-specific split, liner, waistband and artwork directions. Its high-split 2-in-1 reference lists a four-way-stretch shell and a 250 GSM milk-silk liner reference. Confirm the actual fiber composition, weight, liner fit and finishing on the approved sample; a trade name is not a fiber-content declaration.

- View Dazzle Vector training shorts →

## Which product is better for MMA and BJJ training?
There is no universal winner. Custom MMA fight shorts are usually the better starting point for a simple, versatile team or retail SKU. 2-in-1 grappling shorts are usually the better starting point when the buyer specifically wants a built-in liner, closer coverage and a movement-oriented layered construction.
Use this decision table before asking for a quote:
Who should choose custom MMA fight shorts?
Choose custom MMA fight shorts when you need a flexible outer layer for a gym, team, private-label line or multi-purpose training collection. They are also a practical choice when you want to keep the first sample focused on fit, waistband, split, artwork and size grading rather than adding a liner to the development brief.
They may be less suitable if your customer specifically expects built-in compression coverage or if the product concept depends on a layered grappling silhouette. In that case, a 2-in-1 sample may answer the fit question more efficiently.
Who should choose 2-in-1 grappling shorts?
Choose 2-in-1 grappling shorts when the inner layer is central to the product promise: coverage, a close-to-body feel, custom liner artwork or a high-mobility grappling silhouette. TONTON’s listed high-split reference is designed around an ultra-high split and supportive liner, with custom artwork options reviewed during development.
They may be less suitable for buyers who need a pocket, a single-layer shell, a lower side opening or one garment that is accepted under unrelated competition rule sets. The built-in liner is a construction choice, not automatic event approval.
Which product is better for MMA and BJJ training?Buying situation | Better starting direction | Why | Main checks before approval |
MMA striking and mixed training | Custom MMA fight shorts | A simpler outer short can be easier to standardize across a team and retail range | Waist stability, leg clearance, seam comfort, artwork durability and wash care |
BJJ or no-gi grappling training | 2-in-1 grappling shorts when a built-in liner is wanted | The inner layer can provide a close-fitting, coverage-focused feel during scrambles and ground movement | Liner length, compression comfort, heat, waistband security and movement in guard positions |
Competition-oriented development | A rules-specific short brief, not a generic product label | Event requirements can limit colors, pockets, closures, length or underlayers | Current organizer rules, inspection practice, trims, length, color and branding |
Academy team kit | Custom MMA fight shorts or coordinated 2-in-1 shorts | The team can prioritize one consistent fit, logo system and size allocation | Athlete feedback, size grading, repeat-order specification and quantity by size |
Private-label launch | Start with one clearly named hero SKU | One controlled construction makes sampling, product copy and inventory easier | Target customer, return risk, size chart, labels, packaging and reorder feasibility |
High-mobility grappling collection | 2-in-1 grappling shorts | A high-split shell and inner layer can be specified as a dedicated grappling silhouette | Split height, liner behavior, seam strength and whether the event permits the design |

Compare shell clearance and liner fit together when approving a 2-in-1 sample.

## How do competition rules change the product decision?
Check the named event, division and rule edition before approving the pattern, artwork and quantities. The IBJJF uniform page describes permitted colors, pocket and closure restrictions, and shorts length requirements; the exact wording differs by division. For men, it prohibits exposed drawstrings and allows compression shorts beneath the outer shorts in the specified colors.
For amateur MMA, the IMMAF Unified Rules document, identified on the document as being current as of October 2022, includes equipment and kit provisions for official events. It states that approved competition kit and red/blue equipment requirements apply in IMMAF tournaments. Because that document is dated, buyers should confirm the latest federation, national-body and event instructions rather than treating it as a universal current rule.
A useful product brief therefore includes:
IBJJF has also announced changes effective January 1, 2027. Use the edition applicable to the event date, rather than assuming a future change already applies.

- Named organizer or federation: Do not write only “competition legal.”

- Division and market: Requirements can vary by event, division and location.

- Short construction: Record pockets, drawcord position, zippers, snaps, metal, plastic, split and length.

- Color and branding plan: Keep a separate competition colorway if the event requires it.

- Underlayer plan: Confirm whether a built-in liner is allowed, optional or insufficient for the named ruleset.

- Approval evidence: Save the rule URL, access date, artwork version and final sample notes.

- IBJJF uniform requirements →

- IMMAF Unified Rules document →

- IBJJF changes effective January 1, 2027 →

## What should a buyer check in the first sample?
A digital mockup can help approve colors and logo placement, but it cannot confirm fit, hand feel, opacity, liner comfort or seam behavior. TONTON’s sampling and MOQ guide specifically separates mockup review from physical sample review and explains that applicable minimums and timing depend on the selected product and project details.
Use this sample checklist:

- Fit: Measure waist, outseam, leg opening, split height and liner length against a written chart.

- Movement: Test stance, hip rotation, sprawls, shots, guard movement, kicks and scrambling.

- Waistband: Check drawcord position, roll, grip and whether the short stays stable without uncomfortable pressure.

- Layer interaction: On a 2-in-1 sample, check whether the outer shell rides up, twists or exposes the liner in movement.

- Construction: Inspect reinforced seams, hems, print alignment, labels and any trims that could conflict with rules.

- Artwork: Check logo scale, sponsor placement, legibility and color contrast on the actual fabric.

- Sizing: Try the sample on representative athletes and record revisions before grading the full size range.

- Care and labeling: agree fiber declarations, origin and care instructions for the destination market. U.S. care instructions should have a reasonable evidential basis. Review the finished garment and components before approving its washing and drying directions.

- sampling and MOQ guide →

- FTC Care Labeling Rule →
Confirm construction, measurements, artwork and quantities before sampling.

## How should a private-label brand plan the first SKU?
Start with a narrow product architecture rather than launching every silhouette at once. A sensible first range may use one outer custom MMA fight short for broad training and retail appeal, then add a 2-in-1 grappling short as a separate SKU for customers who actively want a built-in liner.
Keep the products separate in your product copy, size chart and SKU records. Do not describe every short as suitable for every competition. Record the approved fabric, measurements, construction, artwork, label, packaging and size breakdown so reorders can be compared with the original sample.
TONTON’s website states that selected custom projects start from 10 pieces and that the target sample window is 3–7 days after product details and usable artwork are confirmed. The site also explains that final MOQ and timing depend on the selected style, materials, construction, artwork and quantity mix. Treat those as project-starting points, not universal commercial terms. Confirm the exact route in writing before committing inventory.
For coordinated tops, review the custom sublimated rash guard program. A team may use a shared logo and color system across a rash guard and shorts while keeping training and competition variants clearly identified.

- custom sublimated rash guard program →

## Key takeaways
Build your TONTON project brief with the intended use, construction, size range, artwork, quantity and destination market.

- Custom MMA fight shorts are usually the simpler, more flexible starting SKU for gyms, teams and private-label ranges.

- 2-in-1 grappling shorts are a dedicated layered option when a built-in liner, coverage and high-mobility grappling silhouette matter.

- Neither construction is automatically legal for every competition; check the current rules of the named organizer.

- A physical sample should validate fit, movement, artwork, trims, labeling and reorder specifications before bulk production.

- A clear brief that separates training, competition-oriented and retail use reduces product-copy risk and avoidable inventory mistakes.

- Build your TONTON project brief →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Are 2-in-1 grappling shorts better than regular MMA shorts?
Not for every buyer. 2-in-1 shorts add a built-in liner and layered coverage, while regular custom MMA fight shorts can be simpler and more versatile. Choose based on intended use, fit preference, rules and product complexity.
Are 2-in-1 grappling shorts legal in every competition?
No. A 2-in-1 construction is not automatically accepted by every organizer. Check current rules for length, colors, pockets, closures, exposed drawstrings, metal or plastic and required underlayers.
Which shorts are best for an MMA gym team?
The best starting product is the one the whole team can fit, reorder and use consistently. Many gyms should compare a simple custom MMA fight short with a 2-in-1 sample, then choose after athlete movement tests and event-rule checks.
Can custom MMA fight shorts be used for BJJ training?
Yes, if the cut, waistband, coverage, seams and movement suit the athlete and the gym’s training format. Training suitability is different from approval for a specific tournament.
What should a supplier include in a fight-shorts quote?
The quote should identify the product construction, material direction, artwork scope, labels, packaging, quantity by style and size, sample charges, MOQ basis, production timing and shipping assumptions.
Is a built-in compression liner the same as competition approval?
No. A liner is a garment feature. Competition approval depends on the named organizer’s current rules, inspection interpretation and the complete garment design.
How many pieces should a private-label brand sample first?
Sample enough to answer the highest-risk decisions: construction, fit, artwork and target customer use. The applicable MOQ and sample route depend on the selected product and project brief, so confirm the commercial terms before scaling.

Page title: Custom No-Gi Grappling Shorts: Rules & Fit Guide

Home/Blog/Fightwear Buying GuideFightwear Buying Guide

# Custom No-Gi Grappling Shorts: Competition Rules, Fit, and Sample Approval Guide
Plan custom no-gi grappling shorts for IBJJF, UWW and training use with a rule-aware brief, fit checklist, artwork review and sample approval steps.
By TONTON · Published November 23, 2026 · 8 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
What are custom no-gi grappling shorts?What does the IBJJF require for no-gi shorts?What does UWW require for grappling uniforms?How do you choose a construction for competition and training?Confirm the measurement chartCheck movement in the intended positionsInspect closures and trimsReview the artwork against the rulesetConfirm the liner and compression planLock the reorder specificationHow can gyms and fightwear brands avoid an expensive wrong order?Key takeawaysBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Custom no-gi grappling shorts should be designed around the event rule set before artwork and bulk quantities are approved. IBJJF and UWW publish different requirements for colors, length, pockets, closures, compression layers and branding, so a short that works for training or one tournament is not automatically legal everywhere. The safest buying process is to confirm the current rules, specify the garment in writing, and approve fit, construction and artwork on a physical sample before production.

TONTON high-split 2-in-1 product reference. A built-in liner and mobility cut do not establish competition approval.

## What are custom no-gi grappling shorts?
Custom no-gi grappling shorts are grappling shorts developed with a team’s artwork, colors, labels, size range and construction requirements instead of selected only from a standard retail size run. They may be used for academy training, competition, team identity, private-label collections or e-commerce sales.
The important distinction is between training-ready and competition-ready. Training shorts can be selected for mobility, comfort, durability and brand appearance. Competition shorts must also be checked against the specific organizer’s current rules. A product label, supplier description or “fightwear” category does not prove approval.
For example, TONTON’s high-split 2-in-1 reference combines a four-way-stretch outer shell, a 250gsm milk-silk inner liner, an ultra-high split, an adjustable drawstring and an anti-slip silicone grip. Those are confirmed product details, but the official product page also tells buyers to check event requirements separately. That distinction should remain in every responsible buying brief.

## What does the IBJJF require for no-gi shorts?
The IBJJF uniform requirements state that men’s no-gi board shorts must use permitted colors, have no pockets or pockets stitched completely shut, and have no buttons, exposed drawstrings, zippers, plastic or metal that could present a risk. The shorts must cover at least halfway down the thigh and must not extend beyond the knee. Compression shorts may be worn underneath in permitted colors.
The IBJJF’s 2027 no-gi rule update takes effect on January 1, 2027, and adds more specific guidance for belt-color visibility and changes the wording around short length. It describes shorts that do not extend beyond the knee, with the bottom no more than 15 cm above the middle of the knee; kids’ divisions must cover at least halfway down the thigh. Because rules can change by edition, division and effective date, verify the current event information before approving a production run.

- IBJJF uniform requirements →

- 2027 no-gi rule update →

## What does UWW require for grappling uniforms?
The UWW 2026 Grappling Uniform Regulations use a different system. The first grappler called wears a red rash guard and the second wears blue. Rash guards must be tight-fitting with short or long sleeves and contain at least 60% of the assigned color. The shorts should match the assigned red or blue color or use a neutral color such as black, white or grey.
UWW also states that grappling shorts must not be excessively baggy or tight, should cover at least two-thirds of the thigh without going below the knee, and should not have pockets or unsafe buttons/snaps. Compression tights under the shorts are mandatory and must reach at least mid-calf. Official competitions also restrict their colors and prohibit bright multicolored patterns.
These differences matter for product development. A high-split 2-in-1 short that works well for training may not match UWW’s required compression-layer arrangement. A vivid academy design may also need a simplified competition colorway for a particular ruleset.

- UWW 2026 Grappling Uniform Regulations →

## How do you choose a construction for competition and training?
Start with the intended use, not the artwork. Use the table below to separate the decision.
There is no single “best” short for every athlete. High splits can suit kicking, sprawls and wide grappling positions, while a longer or more neutral cut may be easier to align with a particular competition rule. For retail, the clearest approach is often to name the use case honestly: training grappling shorts, IBJJF-oriented no-gi shorts, or UWW competition specification, only after the relevant requirements have been checked.
Match the shorts specification to the intended useUse case | Suitable development direction | Main checks before approval | Who it suits | Who should reconsider |
Academy training and open mat | Single-layer or 2-in-1 custom grappling shorts | Mobility, waistband stability, coverage, wash care and graphic durability | Gyms, academies and mixed training groups | Teams that need one garment to satisfy a strict event rule without a rule check |
IBJJF-focused no-gi kit | Rule-aware board-short or permitted compression-short specification | Color, thigh and knee length, pockets, exposed cords, closures and belt-color treatment | Teams competing under current IBJJF requirements | Buyers using one universal design across unrelated organizers |
UWW grappling competition | Shorts plus a separate compliant compression-tights plan | Assigned-color rash guard, shorts proportion, no unsafe trims, tights color and branding placement | Teams entering UWW grappling events | Buyers assuming a built-in liner automatically replaces mandatory tights |
High-mobility MMA or grappling training | High-split 2-in-1 reference or another movement-oriented pattern | Split height, liner coverage, stretch recovery, drawcord, grip and seam comfort | Athletes who prioritize leg clearance and support in training | Buyers who need pockets, lower coverage or a single-layer shell |
Retail or private-label range | A core construction plus separately named competition and training variants | Size grading, style codes, labels, packaging, approved materials and repeat-order records | Fightwear brands and e-commerce sellers | Sellers who describe every variant as competition-approved without event evidence |

## 1. Confirm the measurement chart
Record waist, outseam, leg opening, side-split height, liner length and any tolerance. Do not approve from a product photograph alone. A size chart is a starting point; the sample shows how the pattern behaves on a body.

## 2. Check movement in the intended positions
Test stance, hip rotation, high-knee movement, shots, sprawls, guard work and scrambling. Look for pulling at the crotch, liner exposure, waistband roll, excess fabric and side-split strain. These checks are practical development advice, not a measured performance claim.

## 3. Inspect closures and trims
For a competition specification, review every cord, snap, hook-and-loop component, zipper, pocket opening and plastic or metal part. If the rules prohibit or restrict a feature, remove it from the competition version rather than assuming an inspector will accept it.

## 4. Review the artwork against the ruleset
Prepare separate artwork files when needed. A team may use a bold sponsor-heavy design for training and a simplified red, blue, black, white or belt-color design for a regulated event. Keep the rule reference, artwork version and approval date in the project record.

## 5. Confirm the liner and compression plan
A built-in liner is a construction feature, not universal evidence of competition legality. TONTON lists a supportive 250gsm milk-silk liner on its high-split reference, but the exact fiber record, fit and suitability still need to be confirmed for the selected project. For UWW events, check whether separate compression tights are required.

## 6. Lock the reorder specification
For a gym or private-label brand, retain the approved sample, material record, measurement chart, artwork files, labels, packaging, quantity by size and intended use. TONTON’s custom shorts information recommends reviewing these details as one project specification and confirming minimums by style, design and colorway. Selected projects start from 10 pieces, but that starting quantity is not a blanket promise for every combination.

## How can gyms and fightwear brands avoid an expensive wrong order?
Use a two-version planning method when the team trains in several environments:
For coordinated tops, compare the project requirements with TONTON’s custom sublimated rash guards. For a broader shorts brief, review the custom BJJ and MMA shorts manufacturing page, then use the sampling and MOQ resource to organize quantity, artwork and approval questions.

- Training version: Optimize for comfort, movement, team identity and repeat wear.

- Competition version: Remove uncertain trims, align color and length with the named organizer, and document the exact rule source.

- Shared brand system: Keep the same logo geometry, typography and core color language where the rules allow it.

- Separate SKU and product copy: Do not sell a training short as universally competition legal.

- Sample before scale: Test the physical garment with representative athletes and confirm the final event requirements before bulk approval.

- custom sublimated rash guards →

- custom BJJ and MMA shorts manufacturing page →

- sampling and MOQ resource →

## Key takeaways

- Custom no-gi grappling shorts should be specified by rule set, use case and construction before artwork is finalized.

- IBJJF and UWW requirements are different; do not describe one design as universally competition legal.

- High-split and 2-in-1 features can support training movement, but the liner, colors, trims and length require separate event checks.

- A physical sample, written measurement chart and approved artwork record are essential for gyms, teams and private-label brands.

- The most reliable reorder program keeps training and competition variants clearly named and documented.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Are 2-in-1 grappling shorts legal in every competition?
No. A 2-in-1 construction is not automatically legal in every tournament. Check the organizer’s current rules for pockets, trims, length, colors and whether a separate compression layer is required.
What shorts are allowed under current IBJJF no-gi rules?
Current IBJJF guidance describes permitted-color shorts without unsafe pockets, buttons, exposed drawstrings, zippers, plastic or metal, with length limits around the thigh and knee. Verify the current rulebook and event inspection requirements for your division.
What is the main difference between IBJJF and UWW grappling shorts?
IBJJF and UWW use different requirements for colors, length, compression layers and branding. UWW’s 2026 regulations require assigned-color rash guards and mandatory compression tights, while IBJJF guidance focuses on permitted colors, garment length and safe construction details.
Should a team order one design for training and competition?
Usually not without a rules audit. One shared visual identity is useful, but separate training and competition variants can reduce risk when an organizer restricts colors, length, pockets, cords, branding or under-layers.
What should I send to a custom grappling shorts manufacturer?
Send the intended use, named ruleset, quantity by size and color, artwork files, preferred construction, liner or compression requirements, labels, packaging and delivery target. Ask the supplier to identify assumptions in the written quote.
How many pieces should a gym order for a first custom run?
Use the supplier’s project-specific MOQ and your real size demand rather than choosing a generic quantity. TONTON states that selected custom projects start from 10 pieces, with minimums confirmed by style, design and colorway.
Can custom grappling shorts be sampled before bulk production?
Yes. A sample should be reviewed for measurements, movement, materials, construction, artwork, labels and packaging before bulk approval. A sample confirms the selected project; it does not replace the event organizer’s own inspection or rule decision.
