# How to Build a Private-Label Fightwear Brand Capsule Collection
Build a private-label fightwear capsule with the right products, fabrics, branding, sizing, samples, and launch plan for MMA and BJJ customers.
By TONTON · Published November 16, 2026 · 10 min read · Updated November 19, 2026
IN THIS GUIDE
What should a private-label fightwear capsule include?How do you choose the customer and use case first?Which products should carry the brand identity?How should you compare outer shorts, 2-in-1 shorts, and training shorts?What should you include in a private-label fightwear development brief?How many products should a new brand launch?Why is sampling essential for a private-label fightwear brand?What should you ask an OEM/ODM fightwear supplier before placing an order?Key takeawaysBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
A focused private-label fightwear capsule can start with three product roles: one recognizable short, one coordinated rash guard and one everyday training piece. Choose the assortment around a defined customer use case, then align artwork, labels, sizing and sample approval before expanding. Three roles are a planning framework, not a universal minimum order or launch requirement.

Plan the product range, artwork and branding together before sample approval.

## What should a private-label fightwear capsule include?
A practical first capsule often contains three product roles:
The best mix depends on the business model:
This is a planning framework, not a universal product rule. Your customer profile, sales channel, size distribution, and competition requirements should determine the final assortment.
This structure is useful because each product has a different job. The hero product attracts attention, the rash guard completes the combat-sports look, and the training product broadens everyday use. It also gives a new brand a clearer merchandising story than launching many unrelated cuts and graphics at once.

- A hero product: Usually a custom MMA fight short or grappling short that makes the brand recognizable.

- A matching performance layer: A custom rash guard that carries the same visual identity and serves MMA, BJJ, or grappling customers.

- An everyday training product: Training shorts, a team kit component, or another repeatable item that can be worn beyond competition-style sessions.
Plan a capsule around your business modelBrand situation | Recommended first capsule | Main decision | Less suitable starting point |
MMA gym or academy | Shorts, rash guards, team kit options | Consistent identity across members | A large retail range with many unrelated graphics |
BJJ or grappling team | No-gi rash guard, grappling shorts, training layer | Comfort and team consistency | MMA-only styling that does not fit the academy’s use |
Private-label e-commerce brand | Hero short, matching rash guard, training short | Clear product story and manageable inventory | Ten or more styles before demand is known |
Fightwear brand expanding its range | New short construction plus coordinated apparel | Differentiation from existing products | Copying a competitor’s full assortment without a clear reason |

## How do you choose the customer and use case first?
Start by writing one sentence that describes the first buyer and the moment when the product is used. For example: “Our first collection is for European no-gi academies that need coordinated apparel for training and team events.” That sentence helps prevent contradictory choices later.
Competition requirements should be checked separately from general training needs. Review the official IBJJF uniform requirements, IMMAF competition rules and protocols, or the applicable ADCC event rules. IMMAF’s current rules page links 2021 editions while also listing 2026 summaries; confirm the exact edition, event protocol and permitted apparel with the organizer before approving a competition product.

- Is the product mainly for hard training, competition, travel, team identity, or casual gym wear?

- Will the buyer purchase one garment, a complete kit, or repeat orders for new members?

- Is the collection sold directly to consumers, through academies, or to other brands?

- Which countries will receive the products, and what labeling or event rules may apply?

- Does the buyer expect a conservative team look or a more distinctive retail design?

- IBJJF uniform requirements →

- IMMAF competition rules and updates →

- ADCC rules and regulations →

## Which products should carry the brand identity?
A capsule feels intentional when the same brand system appears across different garments without forcing every item to look identical. Decide the following before final artwork:
TONTON’s custom sublimated BJJ and MMA shorts page is a useful reference point when comparing outer shorts and 2-in-1 constructions, artwork placement, waist details, and size grading. Treat those published configurations as product references to review, not as a substitute for approving your own sample.
For a private-label brand, the goal is not to put the logo everywhere. The goal is to make the product identifiable while keeping the design readable at retail scale and on a moving athlete.

- Primary brand mark: Where is the logo most visible when the athlete is standing, moving, or photographed?

- Graphic language: Will the collection use a geometric pattern, a restrained wordmark, a team crest, or a stronger all-over print?

- Color system: Select one base color, one main accent, and one supporting neutral. This makes later replenishment easier.

- Product hierarchy: Reserve the most detailed artwork for the hero product and simplify secondary pieces.

- Label and packaging treatment: Decide whether the launch needs woven labels, printed labels, hangtags, polybags, or team-specific packing.

- Custom BJJ and MMA shorts development →

## How should you compare outer shorts, 2-in-1 shorts, and training shorts?
The right construction depends on how the customer trains and what level of coverage or layering they prefer.
TONTON’s high-split grappling shorts reference describes a style-specific construction with a stretch shell, compression liner, high split, drawstring, and anti-slip grip detail. These are useful checkpoints for a development brief, but the material and construction should remain SKU-specific rather than being generalized across every short.
Compare shorts construction before approving a collectionConstruction | Strengths | Check before approval | Best fit |
Outer fight shorts | Flexible layering and a familiar MMA silhouette | Waist stability, rise, split, seam comfort, and whether a separate compression layer is expected | MMA training, striking, and customers who choose their own base layer |
2-in-1 grappling shorts | Integrated compression layer and a complete training outfit | Liner coverage, stretch recovery, leg grip, split height, and heat management | Grappling customers who want built-in support and coverage |
Training shorts | Broader everyday use and easier cross-training positioning | Pocket policy, waistband comfort, fabric hand feel, and branding durability | Gym training, warm-ups, and lifestyle-adjacent use |

- High-split 2-in-1 grappling shorts reference →

- How to choose custom MMA shorts →

## What should you include in a private-label fightwear development brief?
A useful brief turns an idea into decisions a manufacturer can review. Include:
TONTON’s custom sublimated rash guard service shows why a rash guard brief should cover sleeve length, panel layout, seam construction, hem control, decoration, labels, and packaging—not just a front logo. For U.S. sales, review the FTC Textile Fiber Rule and the FTC Care Labeling Rule with your compliance adviser before finalizing private-label labels.

- Product category and intended sport or training use

- Outer-only or 2-in-1 construction

- Preferred fit, length, split height, and waistband direction

- Fabric priorities, such as stretch, opacity, drying, hand feel, or recovery

- Artwork files, logo files, color references, and placement notes

- Size range and estimated quantity by size

- Whether the order contains one design, several colorways, or team personalization

- Labels, packaging, destination market, and target launch date

- Competition rules that must be checked, if the product is intended for an event

- Custom rash guard development →

- FTC Textile Fiber Rule →

- FTC care-labeling guidance →

## How many products should a new brand launch?
Launch enough products to tell a complete story, but few enough to sample and replenish responsibly. For many new brands, three core product roles are easier to manage than a broad first catalog. The final number should be based on available development budget, expected demand, size breadth, and whether the products share patterns or materials.
A practical launch sequence is:
This staged approach reduces the risk of tying up cash in too many graphics, sizes, and low-volume variants.

- Validate the hero product. Approve the primary short silhouette, artwork, fit, and size grading.

- Add the matching layer. Develop the rash guard or compression layer with a coordinated visual system.

- Add the training product. Use it to reach gym members who want the brand for regular sessions.

- Measure demand by size and use case. Record which colors, cuts, and sizes create repeat requests.

- Expand only where the data supports it. Add a new construction, team colorway, or seasonal design rather than duplicating the entire range.

## Why is sampling essential for a private-label fightwear brand?
A digital mockup can confirm the concept, but only a physical sample can reveal how the garment behaves on a body. Check the sample while standing, squatting, stretching, drilling, and moving through the sport-specific range of motion.
Use this approval checklist:
TONTON’s sampling and MOQ guide states that selected custom projects can start from 10 pieces and that a physical sample is needed to assess fit, hand feel, opacity, stretch, seams, and workmanship. The same guide distinguishes a digital mockup from a physical sample and says that price, sample charges, packaging, shipping, and timing should be confirmed in a written quote. Treat “from 10 pieces” and a target sample window as project-dependent, not as universal guarantees.

- Fit and size grading across the smallest and largest planned sizes

- Waistband tension, rise, drawstring position, and stability

- Split height, liner coverage, and freedom of movement

- Seam comfort at the crotch, side split, armhole, or waistband

- Opacity and recovery after stretching

- Color appearance under indoor lighting and daylight

- Logo scale, placement, and legibility in photos

- Label position, care information, packaging, and final presentation

- Any sport- or event-specific restrictions

- Sampling and MOQ guide →

- Sample approval checklist →

## What should you ask an OEM/ODM fightwear supplier before placing an order?
Ask for written answers to these questions:
A supplier’s published material or performance description should be read as style-specific unless the written quotation confirms otherwise. The same principle applies to fabric weight, fiber composition, construction, MOQ, and delivery timing.

- Which details are confirmed for this exact style and which are development options?

- What is the minimum quantity by style, colorway, and size allocation?

- What is included in the sample fee and what counts as a revision?

- Which artwork formats are accepted, and who checks production files?

- What labels and packaging can be added for private-label sales?

- What is the quoted production schedule after sample approval?

- How are inspection, packing, shipping, taxes, and duties handled?

- Which details need separate confirmation for different destination markets?

## Key takeaways

- A focused private-label fightwear capsule is usually easier to brand, sample, explain, and replenish than a large disconnected catalog.

- Choose the first products around a defined MMA, BJJ, academy, team, or retail use case.

- Treat outer shorts, 2-in-1 grappling shorts, rash guards, and training shorts as different product decisions.

- Confirm style-specific materials, construction, MOQ, labels, packaging, and timing in writing.

- Use a digital mockup for artwork direction and a physical sample for fit and workmanship approval.

- Check the latest competition rules and destination-market labeling obligations separately from general product development.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
What is private-label fightwear?
Private-label fightwear is combat-sports apparel produced for a brand that sells it under its own name, labels, packaging, and visual identity. The buyer still needs to define the intended use, product construction, artwork, size range, and compliance requirements.
How do I start a private-label fightwear brand?
Start with one customer use case and a focused capsule, then prepare a development brief and approve physical samples before placing a broader order. The first step is assortment clarity, not a large product count.
Is a private-label MMA collection suitable for BJJ customers?
Sometimes, but not automatically. MMA and BJJ customers can share training products, while competition rules, preferred coverage, fit, and visual expectations may differ. Check the exact use case and applicable event rules before combining the categories.
Should I launch custom shorts or rash guards first?
Choose the product that best expresses your customer’s main use case. Shorts may be the stronger hero product for an MMA-focused brand, while a no-gi academy may need a rash guard and grappling short as a coordinated pair.
Is a low MOQ the same as a low-risk launch?
No. A low starting MOQ can reduce the initial quantity, but development costs, size fragmentation, revisions, shipping, labels, and unsold variants still affect risk. Confirm the minimum by style and design in writing.
Do digital mockups replace physical fightwear samples?
No. A mockup checks the visual concept; a physical sample checks fit, stretch, opacity, seam comfort, construction, and workmanship. Approve both before bulk production.
Can I use the same fabric specification for every fightwear product?
No. Fabric weight and fiber composition are product- and style-specific. Confirm the exact material, recovery, opacity, and construction for each SKU instead of transferring a specification from one garment to another.
What information should I send to a private-label fightwear manufacturer?
Ask for the product category, intended sport, estimated quantity, size range, artwork status, destination market, performance priorities, and target date. TONTON’s Project Builder organizes these inputs for an initial project review.

# How to Plan Custom BJJ Rash Guards for an Academy Team
Plan custom BJJ rash guards for an academy or private-label brand with a practical guide to fit, fabric, seams, artwork, sizing, MOQ and samples.
By TONTON · Published November 14, 2026 · 9 min read · Updated November 20, 2026
IN THIS GUIDE
What are custom BJJ rash guards, and how should an academy plan them?How do you define the use before designing a team rash guard?Which fit and sleeve direction should you choose?What fabric and seam details should you compare?How should you prepare sublimation artwork for custom BJJ rash guards?How do you compare a custom rash guard supplier or quote?How many custom BJJ rash guards should an academy order?What should an academy test before approving the sample?Key takeawaysBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Custom BJJ rash guards should be specified around the wearer, fit, sleeve length, fabric, seam construction, artwork, size range and intended order—not selected from a graphic mockup alone. Define use, compare construction options, confirm the written size and material specification, approve a physical sample, then finalize quantities, labels and packaging.

Customer-supplied academy rash guard reference · Artwork and construction are confirmed separately for each project.

## What are custom BJJ rash guards, and how should an academy plan them?
Custom BJJ rash guards are close-fitting grappling tops developed with an academy’s colors, logos, sponsor artwork and chosen construction. The best starting point is not a generic “team shirt”; it is a brief that defines sleeve length, fit, size range, fabric direction, seam placement, artwork, labels and quantity. Academies should approve the physical sample before bulk production, because a digital mockup cannot confirm stretch, opacity, seam comfort or finished fit.
TONTON’s custom rash guard program is presented for BJJ academies, MMA gyms, grappling teams and private-label brands, with selected custom projects starting from 10 pieces; the applicable minimum is confirmed by style, design and order structure.

- Explore custom sublimated rash guards →

## How do you define the use before designing a team rash guard?
Start with the people who will wear the rash guards and the situations in which they will train. A recreational academy order, a competition-oriented team kit and a private-label retail product may share artwork but should not automatically share the same product brief.
Use the intended use to decide what must be tested. Do not describe a fabric as “competition legal” or a garment as approved for a particular event unless the relevant organization has confirmed its current rules. Competition requirements vary, so buyers should check the latest official rules before publishing or ordering for a specific event.
Academy rash guard use casesUse case | Priorities to define | Questions for the brief |
Academy teamwear | Consistent identity, mixed sizes, repeatability and sponsor placement | Adult only or adult plus youth? Names or ranks? One colorway or several? |
MMA or grappling team | Movement, close fit, coverage and frequent training use | Short or long sleeve? What positions should be tested? |
Private-label brand | Repeatable fit block, labels, packaging and customer size coverage | What is the target market and planned reorder structure? |
E-commerce launch | Clear product story, size chart, photography and inventory risk | Which sizes will be stocked first, and what must the sample prove? |

## Which fit and sleeve direction should you choose?
Choose short or long sleeves according to the academy’s training environment, customer preference and layering plan. Fit should be specified with measurements rather than only a market label such as “medium” or “compression.” For a team order, the supplier needs a size range, body or garment measurements, and a quantity-by-size allocation.
A useful fit review includes chest and torso fit without excessive restriction, sleeve length and shoulder reach during pummeling, framing and hand fighting, body length during guard work and positional transitions, neckline comfort, adult and youth grading where needed, and the difference between the digital size chart and the approved physical sample.
TONTON’s published rash guard information describes short- and long-sleeve directions, adult and youth measurements, panel artwork and sample review as part of development. Treat these as project decisions to confirm, not as one universal fit for every customer.

- Compare two-tone long-sleeve rash guards →

## What fabric and seam details should you compare?
A rash guard fabric should balance stretch, recovery, print compatibility, opacity and next-to-skin comfort for the intended use. The exact composition and weight should be recorded for the selected project. TONTON’s rash guard page gives one supplied reference of 220 GSM and 85% polyester / 15% spandex for a stated product direction, while also noting that other weights and blends require separate confirmation.
The published TONTON page describes flatlock seams and an optional silicone anti-slip hem as construction options. It also states that the final composition, weight, measurements and construction are confirmed against the approved sample. No universal breathability or drying rating should be assumed without project-specific testing.
Material and construction checks for custom BJJ rash guardsSpecification | Why it matters | What to verify on the sample |
Fiber composition and GSM | Helps define the material record and compare supplier quotes | Composition, weight tolerance and hand feel |
Stretch and recovery | Affects close fit and repeated movement | Reach, torso rotation and return to shape |
Opacity under stretch | Important for coverage and light-colored designs | Inspect the worn garment under indoor and natural light |
Sublimation compatibility | Supports detailed, all-over team graphics | Color reference, panel alignment and print clarity |
Flatlock seam direction | Can affect skin contact and seam profile | Skin-side comfort, stretch and junction quality |
Mesh option | May be considered for selected panels | Placement, coverage, seam stretch and opacity |
Hem finish | Influences body length and movement | Grip width, skin contact and ride-up during movement |

- Rash guard fabric selection guide →

- Flatlock versus overlock seam guide →

## How should you prepare sublimation artwork for custom BJJ rash guards?
Separate visual design from production instructions. Send vector logos where available, brand color references, sponsor marks, names or numbers, artwork scale, and a front/back/sleeve/panel layout. A supplier should be able to see which graphics are essential, which may move to avoid a seam, and which labels or packaging elements are required.
Before approving a mockup, check whether important logos cross a seam, neckline or curved panel, whether sponsor marks remain readable at the intended size, whether the artwork direction is consistent across adult and youth patterns, whether the same digital color appears appropriately on each selected fabric panel, whether the neck label, size label and care information are included, and whether the artwork version is named and stored for repeat orders.
A mockup answers visual questions. A physical sample answers construction and fit questions. Do not treat approval of one as approval of the other.

- Prepare sublimation artwork →

## How do you compare a custom rash guard supplier or quote?
Ask every supplier to quote against the same brief. This makes differences in MOQ, development scope and delivery assumptions easier to identify.
TONTON’s published sampling and MOQ guide says selected custom projects start from 10 pieces and that the final MOQ depends on product, material, construction, artwork, quantity mix and other requirements. It also publishes a 3–7 day sample target after usable artwork and confirmed details, while noting that sourcing, new patterns and revisions can change timing. Use those statements as starting information and request a project-specific quotation.

- Product direction: short sleeve, long sleeve, adult, youth or mixed team range.

- Quantity: total pieces plus quantities by size and colorway.

- Fabric: composition, GSM or weight reference, stretch and opacity requirements.

- Construction: seam type, panel layout, mesh, neckline and hem finish.

- Decoration: sublimation, logo placement, sponsor artwork and personalization.

- Branding: printed neck label, woven label, care label, packaging and barcode needs.

- Sample: sample charge, sample timing, revisions and approval procedure.

- Commercial terms: unit pricing, shipping basis, destination, duties or taxes and reorder terms.

- Evidence: approved measurement chart, tolerances, material record and production reference.

- Check sample timing and MOQ →

## How many custom BJJ rash guards should an academy order?
Order quantity should follow the academy’s size demand, team structure, replacement needs and cash-flow plan—not an equal number of every size by default. A new academy can use enrollment data and a conservative first run, while an established program can review previous apparel sales and active membership.
A “10-piece starting quantity” does not mean that ten unrelated products, colors or designs automatically share one MOQ. Confirm the minimum for the agreed style, design and colorway in writing.

- Adult and youth sizes where applicable

- Quantity by size and colourway

- Coach or sponsor allocations

- Separate quantities for different sleeve lengths or designs

- Replacement or late-order assumptions

- Packaging and label requirements

## What should an academy test before approving the sample?
Test the physical sample in movements that reflect actual training: pummeling, framing, shrimping, bridging, inversion, guard retention, sprawls and repeated torso rotation. Review both the garment and the artwork.
Only move to bulk production after the sample comments, artwork, measurement chart and construction details are aligned. Retain the approved sample for reorders and reconfirm material availability, MOQ and timing before repeating the order.

- Chest, torso, sleeve and body-length measurements

- Stretch and recovery after movement

- Neckline and seam comfort against the skin

- Coverage when the wearer bends, inverts and rotates

- Print alignment across panels and seams

- Colour against the approved reference

- Adult/youth grading and measurement tolerance

- Hem grip, if included

- Label content, placement, care information and packaging

- Corrections recorded against a dated sample or specification version

- Use the sample approval checklist →

## Key takeaways

- Custom BJJ rash guards should be specified around use, fit, fabric, seams, artwork, sizing and order structure.

- A mockup confirms visual direction; a physical sample confirms fit, stretch, opacity, seam comfort and workmanship.

- A published MOQ or sample target is a starting point, not a universal promise across every style and colorway.

- Academies should keep a written size chart, approved artwork, material record and sample comments for repeat orders.

- TONTON’s custom rash guard information is relevant to academies, MMA gyms, grappling teams and private-label brands, but each project still requires its own confirmed specification.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Can an academy order custom BJJ rash guards with its own logo?
Yes. An academy can develop a team rash guard around its logo, colors, sponsor artwork and selected sleeve direction. Provide usable artwork, size allocations and any label or packaging requirements, then approve the mockup and physical sample before bulk production.
Should a BJJ academy choose short-sleeve or long-sleeve rash guards?
Choose the sleeve length that matches the academy’s training environment, wearer preference and layering plan. Short and long sleeves should be compared through the intended movement and confirmed with the selected size chart rather than assumed to fit identically.
What fabric is used for a custom sublimated rash guard?
A custom rash guard is developed from a stretch performance fabric selected for the project’s fit, recovery, opacity and sublimation requirements. TONTON publishes a 220 GSM, 85% polyester / 15% spandex reference for one stated direction, but the final composition and weight must be confirmed for the selected project.
Are flatlock seams better for grappling rash guards?
Flatlock seams can provide a low-profile construction direction, but “better” depends on seam placement, fabric, fit and wearer comfort. Inspect the skin side, seam stretch and junctions on the physical sample instead of relying on the seam name alone.
Can private-label rash guards include custom labels and packaging?
Yes. Private-label buyers can specify neck-label content, size and care labels, hem branding and individual packing requirements for review. Confirm what is included in the quote and approve the label and packaging details with the sample or production specification.
What is the MOQ for custom BJJ rash guards?
Selected TONTON custom projects are published as starting from 10 pieces, but the applicable minimum depends on style, design, colorway, size allocation and project requirements. Confirm the final MOQ in the written quotation.
How long does a custom rash guard sample take?
TONTON publishes a 3–7 day sample target after usable artwork and confirmed product details are available for selected projects. Material sourcing, new patterns, revisions and special finishing can change the schedule, so request a project-specific date.
Can custom rash guards and grappling shorts use matching artwork?
Yes. An academy or brand can coordinate colors, logos and sponsor direction across the two garments. Each item still needs its own fabric, pattern, size chart, construction checks and sample approval; matching artwork does not mean identical fit or materials. For a coordinated range, review Custom BJJ & MMA Shorts alongside the rash guard brief.

# How to Choose Custom MMA Shorts for Your Brand, Gym, or Team
Learn how to choose custom MMA shorts by fabric, fit, split, waistband, liner, artwork, sizing, MOQ and sampling requirements.
By TONTON · Published November 13, 2026 · 9 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
What should you look for in custom MMA shorts?Choose the right shorts constructionSelect fabric for movement and training comfortDecide between a liner and an unlined shellCheck the waistband and closure systemUse side splits and gussets to improve mobilityPlan sublimation artwork for production, not just for the mockupBuild a practical size and quantity planApprove a sample before bulk productionCustom MMA shorts buyer checklistFinal takeawayBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Start with the intended wearer and training use, then specify the shell, liner, leg opening and waistband. Prepare artwork, quantities and a size breakdown, confirm the applicable MOQ and sample schedule, and approve a physical sample before bulk production.

TONTON tactical stripe camo reference · Compare the leg opening, waistband and hem against your own construction brief.

## What should you look for in custom MMA shorts?
Choosing custom MMA shorts is not only a design decision. The right pair must support movement, stay secure during training, communicate your brand identity and fit your production plan. For a gym, academy, team or private-label fightwear brand, the most reliable process is to decide the use case first, then confirm construction, fabric, artwork and sizing before requesting a sample.
This guide explains the main specifications to review when developing custom MMA shorts, BJJ grappling shorts or a coordinated fightwear collection. Start with six questions:

- Who will wear the shorts? Fighters, grapplers, gym members, coaches or retail customers may need different fits and features.

- Where will they be used? Training, sparring, competition, team uniforms and everyday gym use can require different construction choices.

- How much mobility is needed? Kicks, sprawls, guard work and clinching all place different demands on the garment.

- What artwork must be included? Consider logos, sponsor marks, names, numbers, patterns and repeat-order consistency.

- What quantity and size range are required? This affects the sample plan, grading and final quotation.

- Which rules apply? Always check the requirements of the relevant event, federation or gym before approving a competition product.

## 1. Choose the right shorts construction
Different fightwear constructions solve different problems. The following comparison is a useful starting point for a product brief.
For example, TONTON’s custom range includes standard MMA fight shorts, camo side-split fight shorts and high-split 2-in-1 grappling shorts. The suitable option depends on whether the main priority is unrestricted movement, layered support, team identity or retail versatility.
Compare custom MMA shorts constructionsConstruction | Best for | Main advantages | Points to confirm |
Classic MMA fight shorts | MMA training, sparring and team programs | Lightweight, flexible and easy to customize | Waistband security, side opening and hem finish |
Side-split fight shorts | Kicks, wide stances and movement | Split construction helps leg mobility | Split height, reinforcement and stitching quality |
2-in-1 grappling shorts | Grappling, no-gi training and layered support | Outer shell plus a close-fitting liner | Liner fabric, compression level and waistband comfort |
Custom training shorts | Gyms, fitness programs and warm-ups | Practical for repeated training use | Ventilation, pocket requirements and durability |

- Explore custom BJJ & MMA shorts →

- View tactical camo scallop fight shorts →

- Compare high-split 2-in-1 grappling shorts →

## 2. Select fabric for movement and training comfort
Fabric selection should be based on the intended activity rather than appearance alone. MMA and grappling shorts commonly need a combination of stretch, light weight, drying performance and resistance to repeated washing.
A fabric specification should include composition, weight, stretch direction, finish and approved color references. Avoid approving a product from a photo alone; the fabric hand feel, opacity and stretch recovery should be checked during sampling.

- Stretch: Four-way stretch can help the garment move with the athlete during kicks, sprawls and grappling exchanges.

- Recovery: The fabric should return to its original shape after repeated movement instead of becoming loose.

- Weight: A lightweight shell can reduce distraction during training, while a liner may use a different weight for support and coverage.

- Drying performance: Quick-drying materials are useful for high-sweat training and frequent washing. Confirm the agreed performance requirements.

- Opacity and coverage: This is especially important for 2-in-1 designs and light-colored artwork.

- Print compatibility: Confirm whether the selected fabric produces the desired color, detail and consistency with sublimation printing.

## 3. Decide between a liner and an unlined shell
A liner changes the purpose and fit of the shorts. An unlined shell is often preferred when athletes want a lighter outer layer or plan to wear separate compression apparel. A 2-in-1 style combines an outer short with a close-fitting liner and can create a more complete training product.
For a private-label brand, the 2-in-1 format can also create a stronger product story because the customer is buying a defined system rather than a basic pair of shorts. It is still important to test the product through realistic movements before bulk production. When developing a lined style, confirm:

- Liner length and coverage

- Compression level

- Seam placement

- Waistband connection

- Moisture management

- Whether the liner rides up during movement

- Whether the outer shell and liner artwork need to match

- Review shell, gusset and liner construction →

## 4. Check the waistband and closure system
A fight short can have excellent artwork and still fail if the waistband does not remain secure. Ask your manufacturer to explain the waistband construction and available closure options.
For competition use, hardware and closure requirements may vary by organization. Confirm the applicable rules before finalizing the design. A training product and a competition product should not automatically use the same specification.

- Elastic width and recovery

- Drawcord position and length

- Hook-and-loop or alternative closure design, where appropriate

- Inner waistband comfort

- Branding or label placement

- Whether the waistband works across the full size range

## 5. Use side splits and gussets to improve mobility
Side splits are a visible design element, but they also influence how the shorts move. A higher split may support a wider range of motion, while reinforcement is needed to keep the opening stable after repeated use.
If your design includes a gusset or additional panel, request a clear technical drawing or mockup. Small changes in panel shape can affect mobility, appearance and sewing complexity. Your specification should state:

- Split height

- Front and back length

- Hem shape

- Reinforcement method

- Stitch type and thread color

- Whether the split is symmetrical or asymmetric

## 6. Plan sublimation artwork for production, not just for the mockup
Full-color sublimation allows brands, gyms and teams to create coordinated fightwear with complex graphics. However, artwork must be prepared with production constraints in mind.
Ask for a mockup that shows the artwork on the actual garment panels. Check whether logos cross seams, splits or curved areas. Also confirm how colors will be handled across different fabrics, because the same digital color may appear different on a shell, liner or waistband.
TONTON’s custom project process is designed to align artwork, product construction, fabric direction and commercial details before sampling. This helps reduce revisions when the design moves from a screen mockup to a physical garment. Before sampling, provide:

- Vector logos where available

- Brand color references

- Artwork at the correct scale

- Authorized sponsor logos and their placement priority

- Athlete names or numbers, if required

- A clear front, back, side and waistband layout

- Notes about labels, packaging and repeat orders

- Prepare artwork for sublimation →

## 7. Build a practical size and quantity plan
A good size plan is based on the actual customer or team profile, not an equal number of every size by default. For a gym or academy, collect historical order information when possible. For a new brand, use the expected market and planned size chart as a starting point, then adjust after the first sales cycle.
For selected TONTON styles, the website states an MOQ starting from 10 pieces, while the final quantity, color breakdown and production plan are confirmed according to the brief. Treat published MOQ and sampling windows as starting points, not a substitute for a product-specific quotation. Your order brief should include:

- Adult or youth sizing

- Required size range

- Body measurements and garment measurements

- Quantity by size and color

- Separate quantities for shell and 2-in-1 versions

- Tolerance expectations

- Packaging and labeling requirements

- Read the custom fightwear sampling & MOQ guide →

## 8. Approve a sample before bulk production
A sample should be reviewed as a product, not only as a printed sample. Test the fit and construction through movements that match the intended use: stance changes, kicks, sprawls, hip escapes, clinching and repeated squats.
Only approve bulk production after the final specification, artwork and sample comments are recorded. This creates a reference for future repeat orders. Use this approval checklist:

- Is the waistband secure without uncomfortable pressure?

- Does the side split support movement without opening too far?

- Does the liner stay in place?

- Are seams smooth and reinforced where needed?

- Is the fabric opaque and comfortable after sweating?

- Are logos positioned correctly on the worn garment?

- Are colors acceptable under natural and indoor lighting?

- Does the size chart match the approved sample?

- Are labels, care instructions and packaging correct?

- Use the sample approval checklist →

## Custom MMA shorts buyer checklist
Before requesting a quote, prepare the following information. The clearer the brief, the easier it is for a manufacturer to recommend a practical construction and provide an accurate quote.

- Product type: fight shorts, side-split shorts, 2-in-1 grappling shorts or training shorts

- Intended user: brand customers, gym members, athletes or teams

- Estimated quantity and size breakdown

- Fabric and liner preferences

- Waistband and closure direction

- Split, gusset and reinforcement requirements

- Logo files and artwork references

- Target delivery market and timing

- Label, packaging and private-label requirements

- Competition or organization rules, if applicable

- Start an MMA shorts project brief →

## Final takeaway
The best custom MMA shorts are developed from the athlete’s movement needs, the buyer’s business model and the manufacturer’s production capability. Define the use case, choose the construction, confirm fabric and waistband details, prepare production-ready artwork, plan sizes carefully and approve a physical sample before bulk production.
For brands, gyms and teams starting a custom fightwear project, TONTON can support custom rash guards, MMA and BJJ shorts, training shorts and coordinated team kits. Begin with the product type, quantity, artwork and required timing so the next design and quotation steps can be organized around a clear brief.

- Develop coordinated custom rash guards →

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Are custom MMA shorts suitable for both brands and gyms?
Yes. The same development process can support private-label brands, MMA gyms, BJJ academies, clubs and teams. The difference is usually the quantity plan, artwork system, labeling and repeat-order requirements.
What is the difference between MMA shorts and grappling shorts?
The terms can overlap, but grappling shorts often emphasize movement during ground work and may use a side split, gusset or compression liner. The best choice depends on the athlete’s movement needs and the intended training or competition rules.
Are 2-in-1 grappling shorts better than unlined shorts?
Not automatically. A 2-in-1 design can provide layered coverage and support, while an unlined shell may feel lighter and allow the wearer to choose separate compression apparel. Sample both when the target customer’s preference is uncertain.
What artwork files should I send to a manufacturer?
Send vector logos when available, brand color references, design files, placement notes and any sponsor or athlete personalization requirements. Reference images are useful, but they should be accompanied by a clear list of what must be reproduced.
How many pieces are needed to start a custom order?
The MOQ depends on the product, customization and production plan. TONTON lists selected styles from 10 pieces, with final quantity and size breakdown confirmed after reviewing the project brief.
How long does sampling take?
The sampling window depends on the product, artwork and specification. TONTON lists a target sample window of 3–7 days for selected products after usable artwork and product details are confirmed. Always request a project-specific schedule.
Should I make one sample for every size?
Usually, the first approval focuses on the construction and a representative size, followed by a review of the grading and size chart. For a broad size range or a complex 2-in-1 product, additional size checks may be worthwhile.

# MMA Shorts Construction Guide: Shell, Gusset, Liner & Waist
Compare MMA shorts shells, gussets, side slits, liners and closure systems with real TONTON product examples and a practical sample specification guide.
By TONTON · Published October 29, 2026 · 5 min read · Updated November 18, 2026
IN THIS GUIDE
Select the garment architecture before the artworkRead shell composition separately from stretch claimsUse the crotch gusset to plan movementSpecify side openings by measurementsCompare the waist and closure as a systemDistinguish liner, mesh trim and gussetApprove seams, branding and sport suitabilityBuild a reviewable shorts specificationBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Specify MMA shorts as a complete construction: shell, crotch gusset, leg opening, waist/closure and any liner. A high side split does not replace crotch flexibility, and visible inner mesh does not establish a full compression liner. Select the components for the intended training use, then approve movement, contact surfaces and measurements on the finished sample.

Actual snake-scale sample · inspect the closure overlap, cord routing and inside finishing.

## 1. Select the garment architecture before the artwork
Begin by deciding whether you need an outer fight short, a two-in-one garment with a fitted inner short, or a general training short. These are different development routes even when their graphics look similar. Confirm the intended sport, wearer, fit and any event requirements before selecting details.
TONTON’s references show several useful directions: high-split two-layer shorts, conventional outer fight shorts with a gusset, and training shorts with utility details. Compare physical constructions rather than expecting one style to satisfy every grappling, striking and gym requirement.
Compare TONTON construction referencesReference | Visible / supplied direction | Key approval question |
High-Split 2-in-1 Grappling Shorts | Separate outer shell and 250 GSM milk-silk inner brief | How do liner length, layer attachment and split height work together? |
Snake-Scale MMA Fight Shorts | Hook-and-loop fly, internal drawcord and black gusset reference | Are closure coverage and crotch mobility suitable on the worn sample? |
Cyber-Gradient Training & Fight Shorts | Elastic drawcord waist, curved hem and printed mesh inside hem | Is the inner detail trim or a full fitted liner? |
Functional training shorts | Ventilation and zipped storage details | Are pockets and hardware suitable for the intended training? |

## 2. Read shell composition separately from stretch claims
The snake-scale brief lists a 100% micro-polyester shell and an 88% polyester / 12% spandex gusset. These values refer to different components. The cyber-gradient shell brief is 92% polyester / 8% spandex. They should not be mixed into one generic MMA shorts specification.
Composition alone does not establish tear resistance, drying speed or stretch in every direction. Review the swatch, surface, weight, extension and recovery for each selected shell. Pattern ease and seam placement also influence mobility; fabric stretch cannot compensate for an unsuitable rise or thigh width.

## 3. Use the crotch gusset to plan movement
A crotch gusset is an inserted panel at the junction of the legs. Its dimensions, orientation and seams affect how movement is distributed around the crotch. A stretch-knit gusset can be developed separately from the woven shell; confirm its actual fabric and panel coverage.
Review squats, lunges and the intended kicking or grappling transitions on a fit sample. Look for pulling at the rise, local seam stress, gaps and uncomfortable bulk. A triangular appearance does not establish a particular fabric brand, and the presence of a gusset does not justify a 360-degree mobility guarantee.
Actual Frost White reference · the contrasting gusset makes panel placement easier to inspect.

## 4. Specify side openings by measurements
A side slit or high-split shape opens the outer leg edge. Record its height from an agreed reference, shape, edge finish and reinforcement at the apex. A curved hem and a straight high split are different patterns; an attractive side photograph is not a measurement specification.
Increasing the split can increase exposure or change how the hem moves. On a layered short, compare the split against the inner-short length. Review the opening while standing and moving, then check the edge for rubbing, loose threads or distortion. Agree the finish rather than assuming it is bonded from appearance.

## 5. Compare the waist and closure as a system
An elastic waist with drawcord provides an adjustment route. A hook-and-loop fly with an internal cord uses different components and needs overlap, contact-surface and cord-routing review. Neither should be described as impossible to loosen or open.
For the snake-scale sample, inspect how the hook-and-loop is covered when closed and where the tied cord sits. Review sitting, bending and training movements. On an elastic-waist style, check fit across the size range, twisting, recovery and attachment. Record the garment’s relaxed waist and the agreed fit check separately.

- Check drawcord length, ends and routing on the actual size.

- Confirm closure overlap and covered surfaces.

- Review waist comfort with the intended top or equipment.

- Inspect waistband stitching and attachment after the agreed care review.

## 6. Distinguish liner, mesh trim and gusset
A full fitted inner short is not the same as a mesh panel inside the hem or a crotch gusset. Request an inside-out view and record the complete inner construction. TONTON’s cyber-gradient photos show printed mesh at the inside hem; that alone does not prove a two-in-one compression liner.
The high-split reference uses a separately described 250 GSM milk-silk inner fabric. Milk silk is a supplied trade description, not a complete fiber declaration. Confirm composition, length, fit, leg opening and attachment points. Do not transfer that liner specification to other shorts.

## 7. Approve seams, branding and sport suitability
Inspect the crotch junction, slit apex, waistband, hem and liner joins from both sides. Record the chosen seam construction, reinforcement positions and thread requirements. Decorative stitch rows do not prove a measured seam-strength result.
Confirm any labels, emblems, pockets and hardware against the actual intended use. Competition requirements differ by organizer and can change; obtain the current event requirements for the garment you plan to use. A general MMA or No-Gi label is not event approval.

## 8. Build a reviewable shorts specification
Send a front, side, back and inside view with a measurement chart. At minimum, identify waist, hip, rise, inseam, outseam, leg opening, split height, gusset dimensions and liner length where applicable. State the measurement method and tolerances rather than relying on S/M/L labels.
Keep a versioned record of the approved shell, gusset, waistband, closure, artwork and labels. If you change a component, identify which fit and performance checks must be repeated. This makes the same construction easier to quote, inspect and reorder.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Are higher side splits always better for MMA shorts?
No. Select opening height with coverage, pattern, liner and intended use, then check the worn sample.
Does mesh inside a hem mean the shorts are two-in-one?
No. Confirm whether there is a complete fitted inner short and how it is attached.
Can every training short be used for No-Gi competition?
Do not assume so. Review the actual closure, pockets, hardware and current event requirements.
What measurements should a buyer approve?
Waist, hip, rise, inseam, outseam and leg opening, plus split, gusset and liner dimensions where used, with agreed methods and tolerances.

# How to Choose Fabric for Custom Rash Guards
A buyer guide to rash guard fabric composition, GSM, stretch, coverage and print compatibility, using TONTON’s 220 GSM polyester/spandex reference.
By TONTON · Published October 29, 2026 · 6 min read · Updated November 18, 2026
IN THIS GUIDE
Start with the wearer and intended useRead composition, construction and GSM separatelyCheck stretch and recovery with the actual patternAssess coverage in the selected color and stretchSelect the fabric and print route togetherSpecify mesh, hem grip and seams as separate componentsSend a material approval briefCompare two documented TONTON fabric briefsBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Choose rash guard fabric by matching composition, weight, stretch recovery, coverage and decoration to the intended fit. TONTON’s 220 GSM, 85% polyester / 15% spandex knit is one documented starting point. Approve the actual color, printed fabric and finished garment together; GSM or spandex percentage alone cannot establish comfort, opacity or compression performance.

Supplied garment photograph · 220 GSM main knit; adjacent panels are specified separately.

## 1. Start with the wearer and intended use
A BJJ academy ordering team rash guards and a brand developing a close-fitting gym top may use similar-looking fabrics but need different specifications. Before comparing swatches, identify whether the garment will be worn alone, under a gi, or as part of a matching No-Gi set. Define adult or youth sizing, sleeve length and expected fit.
Describe the movement and coverage you need in observable terms: overhead reach without excessive hem movement, comfortable neck and underarm contact, and coverage when the torso bends. These requirements turn a general request for premium fabric into sample checks. A composition label does not establish medical compression or competition eligibility.

## 2. Read composition, construction and GSM separately
TONTON’s documented main-knit reference is 85% polyester / 15% spandex at a nominal 220 grams per square meter. Polyester content makes it a candidate for sublimation development; the stretch component is only part of the fit equation. Knit structure, finishing, pattern dimensions and sewing also affect how the garment behaves.
GSM describes mass per unit area, not a universal quality grade. Two fabrics with the same GSM can have different thickness, surface, stretch and recovery. A heavier choice is not automatically more breathable, more opaque or more durable. Compare the selected swatches and garments instead of ranking them by weight alone.
How to interpret a rash guard material specificationField | What it tells you | What still needs checking |
Fiber ratio | The declared blend, such as 85% polyester / 15% spandex | Supplier record, label accuracy and decoration compatibility |
Nominal GSM | Fabric mass per square meter | Agreed variation, feel and suitability in the garment |
Knit construction | The material structure | Stretch direction, recovery, surface and seam behavior |
Finishing | A separately specified treatment or surface | Evidence for any claimed drying, UV or antibacterial benefit |

## 3. Check stretch and recovery with the actual pattern
Review stretch in both principal directions and mark the orientation intended for each panel. Stretch is the ability to extend; recovery describes how well the material returns after extension. A swatch that feels very stretchy may still leave a loose neckline or bagging elbows in the finished garment.
Use a fit sample for reaching, torso rotation and the intended training movements. Check the body panels and seams together. If you need a numeric stretch or recovery requirement, agree the test method, extension, load, duration and acceptance criteria before testing. A demonstration video is not a measured result.

- Record the sample size, wearer measurements and intended fit.

- Look for persistent distortion after movement and rest.

- Review seam extension, neckline recovery and lower-hem attachment.

- Recheck when the fabric, pattern or seam construction changes.

## 4. Assess coverage in the selected color and stretch
Coverage must be checked on the finished colorway. Inspect the fabric relaxed and at representative wearing stretch, especially across the chest, shoulders and back. Use consistent lighting and a contrasting background, then repeat on the worn sample.
White, light panels and strongly stretched areas deserve separate review. Do not transfer an opacity observation from a dark sample to every color or size. Record any unacceptable show-through with the location, lighting and stretch condition so the revision can be reproduced.
The supplied label supports the fiber ratio. Nominal GSM comes from the product specification.

## 5. Select the fabric and print route together
For full-panel sublimation, review a printed strike-off on the intended material rather than approving the blank fabric alone. The base color, polyester content and heat response affect the result. Epson explains that conventional dye-sublimation is intended for polyester or prepared substrates and typically uses a light base because the system does not add an opaque white layer.
For a local transfer logo, confirm the transfer system’s compatibility with the blend and wearing stretch. Ask for the actual decoration method rather than treating every heat-applied graphic as the same process. Inspect the printed sample for feel, distorted lines and changes after the agreed care cycle.

## 6. Specify mesh, hem grip and seams as separate components
A 220 GSM main-fabric specification does not identify the mesh insert, silicone hem band or sewing thread. Give each component its own description and placement. For a mesh panel, inspect opening size, skin contact, stretch compatibility and seam junctions.
For silicone anti-slip elastic, confirm width, position, attachment and contact comfort on the worn sample. The band should not be used to compensate for an unsuitable body length. Review seams for profile and extension; a photo of parallel stitches alone is not proof of a particular industrial stitch classification.

## 7. Send a material approval brief
For a first project, request an identified swatch, a printed color sample and a finished fit sample. Keep the accepted versions together. If the color, material finish, panel layout or fit changes, state which checks must be repeated.
A useful brief for this reference is: custom short-sleeve rash guard; nominal 220 GSM 85/15 polyester/spandex knit; identified color and print artwork; agreed size chart; separately specified mesh and hem band; coverage, recovery and care checks recorded before approval. Confirm availability, minimums and sample timing with the project quote.

- Specify product, quantity and size allocation.

- Identify the material and approved swatch version.

- Describe fit, coverage and decoration priorities.

- Record acceptance conditions and unresolved items.

## 8. Compare two documented TONTON fabric briefs
The short-sleeve team rash guard and Jiu-Jitsu Oni long-sleeve rash guard illustrate why GSM belongs to an individual product brief. Both references specify an 85% polyester / 15% spandex blend, but their nominal fabric weights differ. The figures describe development requirements; they do not establish measured abrasion resistance, opacity or compression pressure.
Choose the intended sleeve length, fit and artwork first, then ask for a swatch and garment sample. Confirm the selected fabric identity and weight tolerance, compare stretch and recovery, and inspect coverage in the chosen color under realistic extension. A heavier nominal weight alone is not a pass/fail quality test.
Documented rash guard references — specifications to confirm during samplingReference | Supplied fabric brief | Buyer confirmation |
Short-sleeve team rash guard | 220 GSM; 85% polyester / 15% spandex | Selected fabric, color coverage, stretch recovery and optional hem grip |
Jiu-Jitsu Oni long-sleeve rash guard | Nominal 240 GSM; 85% polyester / 15% spandex | Actual fabric weight, raglan fit, flatlock construction and printed-panel appearance |

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Is 220 GSM always the best rash guard fabric?
No. It is a documented TONTON reference, not a universal optimum. Select weight together with fit, coverage, feel, printing and the intended use.
Does 15% spandex prove four-way stretch or compression?
No. Fiber ratio alone does not establish stretch in each direction, recovery or pressure on the body. Confirm the fabric and finished garment.
Can the mesh insert use the main fabric specification?
No. Mesh, hem elastic and other components need their own specifications.
Can a photo prove opacity in every color?
No. Inspect the selected colorway under representative lighting and wearing stretch.

# Sublimation vs Heat Transfer for Custom Fightwear
Compare dye-sublimation with applied transfer logos for rash guards and MMA shorts: fabric compatibility, artwork, stretch, dye migration and sample checks.
By TONTON · Published October 29, 2026 · 5 min read · Updated November 21, 2026
IN THIS GUIDE
Clarify what the supplier means by heat transferCompare the routes against the designWhen full-panel sublimation is a practical starting pointWhen a local transfer logo may suit the projectKeep printing and fabric transfer distinctApprove a decorated sample through care and movementChoose the route by the whole garmentBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
For custom fightwear, full-panel dye-sublimation is a route for compatible polyester-based fabric and integrated artwork; applied heat-transfer logos add a separate decoration system at selected positions. Both use heat, but their material requirements and approval checks differ. Choose by fabric, design coverage, wearing stretch and the approved sample, not by the word transfer alone.

Actual TONTON printing workshop · printing transfer paper and transferring the image to fabric are separate steps.

## 1. Clarify what the supplier means by heat transfer
Sublimation is itself a heat-transfer process: printed transfer paper is heated against a suitable substrate. In garment purchasing, heat transfer often instead means a logo or graphic applied to the surface, such as a compatible film or printed transfer. Ask the supplier to name the process and material system.
A photograph of a raised logo does not prove silicone, TPU or a particular transfer chemistry. Likewise, a detailed all-over pattern does not prove sublimation rather than another printing or textile process. Record the decoration method in the production specification.

## 2. Compare the routes against the design
The decision starts with the actual garment fabric and artwork. The table describes typical development directions; it is not a universal ranking of durability or price. A transfer suitable for a low-stretch training shell may be unsuitable for a highly extended rash guard panel.
Dye-sublimation and applied transfer logosDecision | Dye-sublimation route | Applied transfer logo route |
Typical scope | Full-panel colors, gradients, names and patterns | Selected logos, names, emblems or graphic areas |
Material choice | Compatible polyester-based fabric; base color matters | Compatibility depends on transfer system, fabric, dye and finish |
Surface feel | No separate graphic film in conventional dye-sublimation | Feel depends on graphic area, thickness and transfer material |
Stretch review | Check printed fabric and garment seams | Check decoration extension, recovery and adhesion |
Main checks | Color, ghosting, alignment, heat effects and panel matching | Edges, adhesion, dye migration, stretch and heat marks |
Cost comparison | Review material, artwork, print and panel work together | Review graphic size, number, preparation and application work |

## 3. When full-panel sublimation is a practical starting point
A polyester-based rash guard with coordinated front, back and sleeve artwork is a candidate for full-panel sublimation. Printing before sewing allows the artwork to be planned around panel shapes. Seams and size grading still require care: a logo that fits one size may approach the seam allowance on another.
Conventional sublimation does not supply an opaque white ink layer. Light-colored compatible fabric is commonly used as the base; darker visual areas can be part of the printed design. Approve the actual printed material because base color and fiber blend affect appearance. Epson’s printing guidance supports these general substrate constraints, not a guaranteed result for every textile blend.

- Check critical colors on the intended fabric, not only on screen.

- Keep small lettering clear of seams and high-distortion areas.

- Confirm intended alignment across panels and realistic variation.

- Review print clarity after the sample is sewn and worn.

## 4. When a local transfer logo may suit the project
A plain shell with a discrete thigh emblem or a limited brand mark may be developed with an applied transfer. Confirm the decoration’s compatible fabrics and extension range, whether a dye-blocking layer is needed, and the equipment settings supplied for that system.
Performance textiles require particular attention to heat sensitivity and dye migration. STAHLS’ performance-wear handbook discusses substrate selection, application instructions and polyester dye migration. A low-temperature or blocking option is system-specific; it is not a universal solution for every fabric.
Leg-emblem reference · approve the actual logo material and application method; appearance alone does not identify the process.

## 5. Keep printing and fabric transfer distinct
TONTON’s published workflow shows roll-to-roll digital printing and a separate rotary heat-transfer stage. The printer produces the transfer-paper output; the heated process transfers the image to suitable fabric. Cutting and sewing then turn the decorated panels into garments.
For a local transfer, confirm where in the garment route application occurs and whether the area can lie flat. Seams, waist elastic and layered panels can change pressure and contact. Do not copy one time, temperature and pressure setting across unrelated fabrics or transfer products; follow the selected system’s instructions and approve the result.

## 6. Approve a decorated sample through care and movement
Start with the identified fabric, dye color and decoration system. Check appearance after the recommended curing or settling period, then review normal wearing stretch and the agreed care procedure. Reinspect color change, transfer edges, surface feel and garment distortion.
Do not promise permanent color or a fixed number of washes without an appropriate report. A practical sample check can reveal a problem but is not a substitute for a specified laboratory method when a customer requires formal performance evidence.
Decoration approval recordCheck | Record before approval |
Material and method | Fabric reference, color, transfer/ink system and sample ID |
Artwork | Version, dimensions, position and panel alignment |
Visual result | Color reference, sharpness, heat marks and ghosting |
Movement | Intended extension and observed recovery or edge issues |
Care review | Washing/drying conditions, cycle count and observations |
Decision | Approved version, corrections, retest needs and approver |

## 7. Choose the route by the whole garment
For full-body team artwork, start by assessing sublimation on the selected polyester-based knit or woven. For a limited logo on an existing plain garment direction, review a compatible transfer system. A mixed approach is possible, but each additional process needs its own approval and cost review.
Send the supplier the garment reference, fabric, graphic files, quantity per design and intended placement. Request a process recommendation with a sample plan. This is more useful than asking which technique is always cheaper or always lasts longer.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Is sublimation different from heat transfer?
Sublimation uses heat transfer, but buyers often use heat transfer to mean a separate surface-applied logo. Specify the actual process.
Can I sublimate directly onto any dark rash guard?
Conventional dye-sublimation does not add an opaque white layer. Confirm the base fabric and design route rather than assuming an existing dark garment will reproduce the artwork.
Will a local transfer stretch with a rash guard?
Only if the selected system is compatible with the fabric and required extension. Approve the decorated garment through movement and care checks.
Which process costs less?
Compare the complete specification, quantities, artwork coverage and application work. There is no universal price winner.

# Custom Rash Guard & MMA Shorts Sample Approval Checklist
A practical sample approval checklist for custom rash guards and MMA shorts: materials, measurements, artwork, seams, closures, care and versioned sign-off.
By TONTON · Published October 29, 2026 · 5 min read
IN THIS GUIDE
Freeze the reference before checking the garmentCheck material and component identityMeasure consistently and record actual valuesInspect the product-specific risk pointsApprove artwork, labels and packing togetherUse the approval checklistDefine care checks without inventing a test resultSign off a version, then control changesBuyer questionsDiscuss your specification →THE SHORT ANSWER

## What buyers need to know
Approve a custom fightwear sample against a controlled reference: material record, artwork version, measurement chart, construction notes, labels and packaging brief. Record actual observations and required corrections, then approve a named sample version. A mockup approves layout; it cannot establish fit, hand feel, seam comfort or the finished garment’s behavior.
Open the approval checklist ↓
Production inspection photograph · sample approval should record the same measurement points used for bulk inspection.

## 1. Freeze the reference before checking the garment
Assign a sample ID, date, style, color, size and revision number. Attach the current artwork and measurement chart. Identify which fabric, decoration and construction the sample represents, plus any substitute components that will change before production.
Separate a mockup, a fit sample, a decorated sample and a pre-production reference if they represent different stages. One sample should not silently approve a detail it does not include. List outstanding items so the buyer and factory know whether bulk production is authorized or still on hold.

## 2. Check material and component identity
Match the main fabric with its identified swatch and supplied composition/GSM record. Inspect color and surface, then check stretch direction, recovery, feel and coverage under the agreed conditions. Photographs and a label can support review but cannot establish every performance claim.
Record separate specifications for mesh, liner, gusset, hem elastic and closure components. For example, the rash guard’s 220 GSM main-knit brief does not identify its mesh, while a fight short’s shell composition does not identify its gusset. Note any mismatch before approving the garment.

## 3. Measure consistently and record actual values
Lay the garment as agreed without unintended stretching. Use a defined point-of-measure diagram so both parties measure from the same locations. Record the sample size, target, tolerance and actual measurement for each point. A photo should show the tape endpoints if it is used to resolve a discrepancy.
For rash guards, include body length, chest width, hem opening, sleeve and neck details as appropriate. For shorts, include waist, hip, rise, inseam, outseam and leg opening, with liner and split dimensions where applicable. Do not approve every graded size solely because one medium sample fits.
Measurement record templatePoint of measure | Target | Agreed tolerance | Actual / result |
Style / sample size / revision | Enter reference | Not applicable | Enter sample ID |
Chest or hip width | Enter value + unit | Agree before approval | Record actual |
Body length or outseam | Enter value + unit | Agree before approval | Record actual |
Waist / hem / leg opening | Specify relaxed or extended condition | Agree method and range | Record actual |
Sleeve / inseam / split / liner | Use relevant garment points | Agree before approval | Record actual |

## 4. Inspect the product-specific risk points
Turn the sample inside out and inspect the seam junctions, edges and attachments. For a rash guard, pay attention to underarms, neckline, sleeve joins and hem band. For shorts, inspect the crotch, gusset, side-opening apex, waist, closure and inner-layer attachment.
Wear-test the intended movements and identify the size and wearer. Record rubbing, pulling, exposed closure surfaces or distortion by location. A comfortable fit session does not prove tear resistance or long-term wash durability; formal requirements need an agreed method and evidence.
Actual snake-scale sample · inspect the closure overlap, cord routing and inside finishing.

## 5. Approve artwork, labels and packing together
Compare logo scale, placement, colors and spelling with the approved artwork version. Check critical panel crossings on the assembled garment. A screen mockup cannot guarantee the printed color, and a clean print swatch cannot guarantee alignment after sewing.
Check size labels, composition and care information against the actual materials and the destination brief. Confirm folding, bags, size allocation and carton requirements. Where destination-specific labeling obligations apply, assign responsibility for checking the applicable requirements rather than treating this checklist as a universal compliance certificate.

## 6. Use the approval checklist
Record Pass, Revise, Not checked or Not applicable for every relevant row. Add a photograph or measurement reference and the owner of each corrective action. Resolve revisions before the final sign-off; do not leave blank fields that could be mistaken for approval.
Sample approval checklistArea | What to check | Record / outcome |
Reference control | Style, size, color, sample ID and revision | Version and date |
Materials | Main fabric and each separate component | Swatch / specification ID |
Measurements | Agreed points, method and tolerances | Targets and actual values |
Fit and movement | Representative wearer and training movements | Location of pulling or rubbing |
Coverage | Selected color, lighting and wearing stretch | Conditions and observations |
Print / logos | Artwork version, scale, position and colors | Approved reference / corrections |
Seams / edges | Skipped stitches, openings, puckering and junctions | Issue location and photos |
Waist / closure | Cord, elastic, overlap and contact surfaces | Function and fit observations |
Inner layer / gusset | Length, coverage, recovery and attachment | Component-specific result |
Care review | Agreed washing / drying and review conditions | Conditions, cycles and observations |
Labels / packing | Confirmed text, size mix and packaging | Approved files / allocation |
Final release | Corrections completed and correct version retained | Approve / hold, approver and date |

## 7. Define care checks without inventing a test result
Agree washing, drying, review timing and the number of cycles before testing. Record dimensional change, appearance, color, seam condition and decoration issues. Keep the initial dimensions so the result can be compared with the same reference.
AATCC TM150 addresses garment dimensional change after home laundering, but its public scope notes limitations for some stretch fabrics. A qualified testing provider should confirm the appropriate method and acceptance criteria for the actual garment. The existence of a standard does not mean this sample has been tested or certified.

## 8. Sign off a version, then control changes
The approval record should identify the accepted sample and attachments, approver, date and decision. State whether approval covers fit, decoration, all components or a limited stage. Keep one reference accessible to the buyer and the factory.
A change in fabric, artwork, fit, closure or labels after approval should trigger a documented review. Bulk QC then checks production against the accepted specification and sampling plan. Sample approval and final shipment inspection serve different purposes; keep both records.

BUYER QUESTIONS

## Before you approve the next step
Can a digital mockup replace sample approval?
It can approve layout, but it cannot confirm material feel, fit, movement or finished workmanship.
Should every sample use fixed universal tolerances?
No. Agree tolerances by measurement point, material and product before approval.
Does approving one size approve the full size range?
Not automatically. Agree the grading and which sizes need physical review.
Is this checklist a laboratory certification?
No. It is a project approval framework. Formal test claims require the applicable method and report.
